The remedy is promotion, not verification: a decision that will outlive the unit becomes a decision note; an owner's call becomes an open question on the arc; decided-but-unbuilt work becomes an increment on its arc. Leave a pointer where the prose was, not a copy.
fields.description: A decision not to build, written into a medium with no status and no owner, cannot be told apart from unfinished work — promote it into a status-bearing record.

fields.why: Research on agents working under standing rules found nearly every failed run claiming compliance while citing the rules it broke: agent self-reports are routinely, confidently wrong. The store can say which session wrote a record and never whose call it was, so the human's own words are the only thing a later reader can weigh independently of the agent's conclusion. An empty field reads as weak; a reconstruction reads as evidence it is not, and the moment it came from cannot be re-run.
fields.title: A human's words are stored verbatim, or not at all
fields.statement: A field whose job is to durably record what a human said — a re-steer's evidence, an owner's directive on a decision, a quoted answer — holds the exact words or stays EMPTY. A paraphrase, summary or reconstruction in that field is a defect, not a weaker filling, because every record is typed by an agent and an agent's own account is the least reliable artifact in its trajectory.
fields.howToApply: Test: could the human read the field back and recognise it as what he said? If not, leave it empty and record the weaker, honest form instead (e.g. mark the basis agent-derived). Keep the human's words and the agent's account in separate fields (evidence vs self-report), never one field with a convention. When a schema refuses a missing quote, word the refusal to name the honest weaker record, not just 'required', or authors learn to fill it. Never backfill a verbatim field from a summary. Scope is narrow: durable stored evidence of an utterance only — debriefs, handovers and note bodies should summarise for their reader.
fields.description: A field that durably records what a human said holds his exact words or stays empty — a paraphrase in it is a defect, never a lesser filling.

fields.title: A measured claim carries the method that produced it
fields.problem: Numbers on a moving surface are supposed to change; the defect is that a later reader cannot tell from the note whether a figure was a reproducible measurement or a one-off snapshot, so before checking it they must reconstruct the measurement by guessing what was counted. In 0.2 an audit found 2 of 4 open questions drifted, one moving from 'n=1, self-measured' to 'n=43 sessions, 1 independent hit' within three days, unnoticed until someone went looking. The author is the only party who holds the method for free.
fields.approach: Beside each live figure, in the same field (not a footnote — a method kept elsewhere drifts from the number it describes), name: (1) the instrument, runnable verbatim — e.g. `storytree library list question`; (2) the sample and what it counts; (3) the moment, when the surface moves independently of any diff. At re-verification, the annotation is the instruction: re-run what it names; if it names no instrument, re-measure rather than re-read. When the figure moved, correct it in place AND re-stamp the method. Do NOT annotate figures that are not readings of a moving surface — a count fixed by a decision, a quoted constant — that is noise that trains readers to skip the annotation.
fields.statement: Any live, measured figure written into a durable note — an open question's stakes, an arc's intent or end state, a re-verification — is written together with its METHOD: the command or query that produced it, the sample (n, and n of WHAT), and when it was taken. If there was no instrument, say so: 'self-measured', 'eyeballed', 'filer's self-report'.
fields.tradeoffs: A parenthetical per figure, written while the author holds the method for free, against a reconstruction every later reader pays. It detects nothing and makes no claim true — it only makes every drift check cheaper. Nothing enforces it; a check keyed on backticks or 'n=' would be trivially satisfiable.
fields.description: A live number written into a durable note travels with how it was measured, so the next reader can re-run it instead of reconstructing it.

fields.why: In 0.2 an implementing agent built a described-but-uncontracted slice three times on one capability, even though the passage carried a plain not-yet-contracted label; each run passed honestly on the test it wrote, and the briefed contract showed up merely as uncovered. Deleting the future-slice prose and re-running built the briefed contract first time.
fields.title: A spec body describes only what it contracts
fields.statement: A capability's body carries only behaviour that is under contract. Anything described concretely enough to implement will be read by the implementing agent as something to build, and it outweighs the brief because it is the more specific thing in context. Labelling a passage 'later' or 'not yet contracted' does not defuse it; the only reliable fence is its absence. Direction and future slices belong on the story or on an arc's increments.
fields.howToApply: Before handing a capability to an agent (or yourself) to implement, read its body as a to-do list and strike anything implementable that is not a contract. Move durable intent to the story and sequencing to an arc increment. If an uncontracted slice has already been built, adopt it as a real contract so the work is kept, and remove every remaining mention of it from the body so the next run is not re-baited.
fields.description: An implementing agent reads a capability's body as instruction: a concretely described but uncontracted behaviour gets built instead of the contract it was asked for.

fields.why: Accepted decisions are what a new session calibrates to, so stale-but-accepted prose is read as live guidance — even an answer found in a decision may be dead. A correction left undone misleads every future reader, while removing overtaken prose costs nothing the history does not already hold. In 0.2 hundreds of amended decisions carried no note in their own body, and well-annotated ones still opened with the false sentence, so readers stopped at it. Escalating instead of correcting is free for the session and costly for the owner.
fields.title: Accepted decisions carry no stale prose
fields.statement: Every accepted decision in the current set is true in full. The moment a claim in one is overtaken, make it true again, choosing the operation by intent: if the DECISION did not change, CORRECT the body in place (the library's history keeps the prior text); if it did, write a NEW decision that supersedes the old, which then reads as superseded and stays as a browsable record. A decision that narrows or retires a clause of a standing one annotates that clause in the target, in the same landing. Durable cross-cutting guidance found in a decision body is rehomed into the principle, definition or pattern that owns it.
fields.howToApply: Ask whether the reasoning a clause rests on still holds; 'accepted' only proves nobody has checked. Then ask: did the decision change? No → edit in place. Yes → new decision with a supersedes edge. For a narrowed clause, put the note where the clause OPENS (who amended, when, what is dead, what replaced it) — a false opening sentence with its correction six lines below still misleads. A plain 'this rests on that' link obliges no annotation and never makes its target load-bearing. Status flips, edge fixes and typos are in-place too. When in doubt, treat it as a re-decision or ask; never silently rewrite what was decided.
fields.description: An accepted decision is true in full: overtaken content is corrected in place, a genuine re-decision supersedes, and a narrowed clause is annotated where it sits.

fields.steps:
1. Ask, do not infer: the first line of `pnpm test` is the `scope:` decision; `pnpm test -- --scope` prints it and runs nothing. `--full` forces everything; `--only=<pkg>` and `--rerun-failed` re-run just part.
2. The change set is merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) against the working tree, untracked files included; each file maps to its package, then dependents are added by declared dependency OR by a relative path in code that reaches another package.
3. It fails wide: a root file, any package.json, the lockfile, scripts/**, a file in no package, a missing origin/main, or no change at all runs everything. A root path is narrowed only once its test-time readers were measured, never by guess.
4. There is ONE decider (scripts/test-scope.mjs). Never write a second classifier for CI or a tool - two that agree today drift tomorrow, and a local pass stops predicting a CI pass.
5. If your change makes a package read another package's files with no dependency or relative-path edge the scope can see, declare the edge - otherwise a change there skips your tests and main goes red later.
6. Pushes to main run full (merge-base is HEAD itself); an automerge makes no push run, so a narrow PR's full proof comes from the next push to main.
fields.title: Affected-only test scope
fields.trigger: Every `pnpm test` run, locally and in CI. Read this when asking why a run tested only some packages, when adding code that reads a file in another package, or when main goes red soon after a narrow merge.
fields.surfaces: `pnpm test` (scripts/test.mjs, scripts/test-scope.mjs), CI's `pnpm test` step on three OSes, `.pgtest/last-run.json` for re-runs.
fields.statement: `pnpm test` runs only the workspace packages holding a changed file plus every package that depends on them, and CI runs the very same command, so a local run and CI decide identically. Anything the workspace graph cannot account for runs everything. A narrow green proves the reached packages, not the workspace.
fields.description: How `pnpm test` narrows to the packages a change can reach, what forces the full run, and how to read a narrow green.
fields.failureModes:
- Reading a narrow green as a full-workspace proof.
- A cross-package file read with no edge: the one shape that lets an untested change merge.
- Quietly loosening a fail-wide rule to save minutes.
- Moving code into its own package to shrink a run: dependents still run it; packaging buys a boundary, not a smaller suite.

fields.rule: Some verdicts are the owner's by nature: "it looks right", "it works live", "this spend is fine". An agent may prepare them — stand the experience up, verify it serves, hand over a working link and what to look at — but it never records the verdict itself, never marks work healthy on its own say-so, and never reports "attested" for something only it has seen. Where a test can prove the behaviour, prove it that way instead; where none can, the gap is the owner's to close.
fields.title: An agent never self-attests
fields.statement: An agent never grants itself an owner-only attestation; it stages the experience and the owner signs.
fields.enforcedBy: Discipline. 0.3 has no signed-verdict spine; the owner's sign-off is given in person or as the answer to an open question, and nothing mechanical detects a self-granted one.
fields.description: A verdict only the owner can give — a look, a feel, a live check, a spend — is never granted by the agent that did the work.
fields.failureMode: An agent vouches for its own unproven work, so a surface with no honest test reads as healthy and the proof means nothing — the reason 0.2 kept attestations in a log that could never reach healthy.

fields.why: Ending a turn in a wait state is the one failure an agent cannot recover from itself: it has no further turn in which to notice. Measured in 0.2: a child agent asked to run a ~100-second command backgrounded it unprompted, announced it was waiting, and ended its turn — the file was never written, and the report landed at a session that had never spawned it, which had to relay it. Lanes whose briefs told them to poll in-turn did not stall; lanes without that line did.
fields.title: An awaited notification is never a turn-ending state
fields.statement: An agent that dispatches asynchronous work — a background subagent, a background shell task, a spawned helper — never ends its turn awaiting that work's completion notification. The signal is addressed to you, but it is delivered at your NEXT tool round-trip; an agent that stops taking tool calls stops being addressable, and the result surfaces at the nearest still-live ancestor instead. Keep taking turns while you can bound the wait; when you cannot, finish on your own judgment and hand back a dispatch handle.
fields.howToApply: Before returning, ask: does anything here depend on a result I dispatched and have not read? If you can bound the wait, keep working and read the work's real terminal state (exit status or a sentinel file), not a line scraped from its log; never let one capped foreground call be the only thing holding long work. If you cannot bound it, return now and say what was dispatched, WHERE its verdict will appear (a path agreed in advance), and that it is UNVERIFIED — never a pass. Never re-spawn a helper whose result has not reached you. If a completion report arrives for work you did not commission, relay it to its dispatcher and tell it to act on its own judgment this turn.
fields.description: Never end a turn waiting for a notification from work you dispatched — delivery rides your next tool call, so ending the turn forfeits the result.

fields.why: Substituting a correlated signal is cheap and usually right, and it fails silently in exactly the cases the mechanism existed for. In 0.2 a worktree reaper keyed its idle clock on a git reflog mtime; one git maintenance pass rewrote it in 31 of 39 worktrees at once, so nothing ever aged out. An install check keyed on node_modules PRESENCE rather than CURRENCY, so a lockfile that moved surfaced later as an unrelated-looking missing module. A pre-run idle probe certified a quiet box at t0 while sibling sessions loaded it during the timed run.
fields.title: An observable is evidence only for what it observes
fields.statement: Name the property first, in one sentence with no mechanism in it. Then a check, staleness heuristic, cleanup clock or exclusion (claim, lock) must key on something that can SEE that property — not something that usually travels alongside it. And a measurement is evidence only for the operation, surface and interval it actually covered; a reading at one moment is not evidence about a whole run.
fields.howToApply: Name one ordinary operation that moves your key without moving the property, or the property without the key; if you can, the key is wrong. An mtime sees 'written', not 'changed'; presence sees 'once done', not 'current'; a claim on a parent sees the parent, not each child — a coarse key standing in for a set does not fence the set. An exclusion that fences nothing looks identical to one that works until it is made to refuse, so a quiet history is no evidence. When citing a figure, state exactly what was measured and narrow the claim to that. When timing on a shared machine, bracket the whole interval, not just its start.
fields.description: A check must key on something that can see the property it gates, and a number is evidence only for what it measured, over the interval it spanned.

fields.why: A durable record keeps the WORDS and silently drops the THING, and the loss is invisible: the citation still reads like a reference, so the next session reconstructs a plausible DIFFERENT surface from the prose — worse than a blank because it looks finished. In 0.2 an owner-approved playable composition was cited only by a local path; a later session built a dashboard instead, costing an owner interruption and a full rework.
fields.title: An owner-approved reference is repo-resident
fields.statement: When the owner approves something you can render, replay or look at — a mock, a render, a playable composition, a style reference — commit it to a repo path in the same change that records the approval, and cite it by that path from the arc, decision or story that carries the intent. A scratchpad path, a chat attachment, a local file or a live URL leaves the next session only the prose.
fields.howToApply: At any handoff after an owner approval, ask: could a session holding only this repo and this citation open the exact thing approved? If it depends on your machine, a transcript, an attachment or a running server, commit it (e.g. under docs/design/<topic>/) and replace every ephemeral handle with the repo path. Keeping file lists out of durable notes is about prose, not about the artifact — the note carries the pointer, the repo carries the thing. Committing a reference is not approving it; the owner still signs the look.
fields.description: An owner's approval is only as durable as the artifact it was given to: commit the approved thing and cite it by repo path.

fields.why: Surface data is the fastest-rotting prose in a corpus: files move and packages dissolve, and a stale file list misleads silently because the reader cannot tell truth from rot. 0.2 repeatedly had to evict execution prose from decision bodies for this reason; its attempt to keep surface in anchored, freshness-checked plans did not last.
fields.title: Durable notes carry intent, not implementation surface
fields.statement: Implementation surface — file lists, package paths, expected edit footprints, ordering over concrete code — does not go into a durable note: a decision, story, capability body, principle, definition or arc intent. Those carry intent, outcomes and pointers. Where a durable note must name code, name the owning SURFACE (a command, a package, a check), never an enumerated file list. Surface detail belongs in things that are honestly short-lived: the PR, the commit, the working session.
fields.howToApply: About to write a path, package list or edit footprint into a note? Ask: would this still be true in a month, and would the reader notice if it were not? If not, put it in the PR description or leave it to the code, and keep the note to intent plus a pointer to the owning surface. This is about prose: an artifact the owner approved is still committed and pointed at.
fields.description: File lists, package paths and edit footprints rot fast; a durable note carries intent, outcomes and pointers, and names code only by its owning surface.

fields.steps:
1. Do not punt it: "you should now run X" makes a solo owner context-switch to a terminal for a command you could have run (the owner asked for this after an infra apply was handed back to him).
2. For irreversible changes, preview first - a plan, dry-run or diff - so the owner approves a concrete change.
3. Issue the action and let the permission prompt be the approval surface; where no prompt applies, ask one inline yes/no.
4. Keep the decision with the owner every time: you make approval one click, you do not remove it.
fields.title: Attempt privileged actions, approve inline
fields.trigger: A unit reaches a step that needs the owner's go-ahead: an irreversible, outward-facing or otherwise privileged action.
fields.surfaces: The session's own tool calls and the harness permission prompt (or an inline question). Writes nothing to the library.
fields.statement: For an action that needs owner authorization - a deploy, an infra change, a `gh` mutation, anything outward-facing or hard to reverse - issue the tool call yourself so the harness raises its permission prompt, or ask one short inline yes/no. The owner still decides; this changes the mechanism, not who signs off.
fields.description: When an action needs the owner's go-ahead, attempt it and let approval happen inline - never decline in prose and hand the command back.
fields.failureModes:
- Declining in prose and handing the command back.
- Reading this as auto-allow and widening harness permissions on its strength.
- A blind apply with no preview.
- Deciding an owner-owned irreversible action yourself because approval is "just one step".

fields.why: Derived sources lag: prose lags the decisions it summarises and generated guidance lags the library it is rendered from. In 0.2 a grep hit inside a comment scoped work to the wrong package; a brief and an offline listing 'agreed' a note did not exist while the live store held it — two views of one stale snapshot counted as two witnesses; a handoff said a PR had landed while its branch did not yet exist on the remote, one step from a duplicate build.
fields.title: The authoritative source beats the derived one
fields.statement: Resolve every factual question to the source the system ENFORCES — the one that would fail a load, a validation or a build if it were wrong — not one that merely mentions the fact. The library beats a generated file or a doc that quotes it; the schema beats prose about valid fields; a package.json beats a grep for its name; the git remote's branch and merge state beats a handoff saying 'it landed' and beats your own checkout. Run this before a disagreement is visible, not only after.
fields.howToApply: Before asserting something, ask which source enforces it and read that one. Treat a second source as corroboration only if it could have disagreed — two views of one snapshot are one observation. Treat any reading of a shared, moving surface ('X does not exist', 'there are 9 open', 'Y has merged') as a timestamped state claim that expires; re-read it against the enforced source immediately before acting on it, hardest when acting on it is the job (authoring the missing thing, publishing the figure, escalating a block). A claim you were TOLD rather than saw is in-flight, not landed — wait on it or ask, don't rebuild it. Name any disagreement you find.
fields.description: When sources disagree — or before you rely on one — resolve to the source the system enforces, not the one that merely mentions the fact.

fields.why: In 0.2 one accepted decision said its predecessor named 'three' failures while quoting that predecessor's own sentence, which named two — citation present, quote accurate, characterisation false — leaving two accepted records contradicting each other. Another write-up said a decision 'already supplies' a fence when the decision only said the change 'may' be made 'as its own increment'; it never landed. Decisions are required to characterise each other, so this recurs by construction, and nothing checks it.
fields.title: Citing a document is not reading it
fields.statement: A claim about what another document says — how many instances it named, whether a decision permitted or required something, what it concluded — is derived from that document, and a citation is not a reading: the reference travels with the claim, makes it look checked, and nobody follows it. Open the passage you are characterising before you write the sentence, and before you rest a move on someone else's.
fields.howToApply: Ask of your own sentence: am I QUOTING this document or DESCRIBING it? A quote you verify by copying; a description ('X decided', 'already covers', 'names three', 'the spec requires') only by reading around it — so open it and count or quote what is actually there. Quoting a line does not exempt the summary of its paragraph. Read a decision's modal verbs as load-bearing: 'may', 'lands as its own increment', 'reserved' are permissions and deferrals, not landings.
fields.description: A sentence describing what another document says is derived from it, and the citation riding alongside makes it look checked — open the passage before you write the sentence.

fields.why: On a surface several stories render, a change can look like the flagship story while its writes land in files another capability owns. Sessions that claimed by resemblance in 0.2 left the true owner's lane reading free while work was happening inside it — and the ledger cannot catch that, because a claim on the wrong unit is unique and succeeds. A fence only means something if a refusal is honoured.
fields.title: Claim by write-ownership — the capability you will write
fields.statement: Route claims by write-ownership, not resemblance. Before starting, resolve which capability owns the files the work will actually write, and claim it through the agent link; claim every capability you will write, and claim the increment you are driving when there is no capability to name. A refused claim binds: stop working that unit. A claim conflict is never an owner question.
fields.howToApply: Find the owner from where the files live (in 0.3, one package per story, so the package tells you the story; then name the capability inside it). Claim every capability you will write, or the increment when none applies. If a claim is refused, read who holds it and why, then either work another unit you already hold, or write your residue onto the owning arc, release your claims and end — never build around the fence, never idle waiting, and never escalate it to the owner. If two genuinely disjoint pieces of work keep colliding on one capability, that capability is drawn too coarse: raise it as a story-shaping question.
fields.description: A session claims what it will WRITE: the capability that owns the files it will change, every one of them, or the increment it is driving when no capability can be named.

fields.why: Self-containment is what lets a story be rebuilt, re-proven or ported without spelunking its neighbours' internals. storytree 0.3 is itself a port of behaviour, not code, from 0.2 — exactly the rebuild this guideline makes cheap, and exactly what becomes expensive where a story's meaning lives only in its code or its neighbours.
fields.title: Cold rebuild
fields.statement: A story should be written so that a cold agent — given only the story's own spec and contracts plus the DECLARED interfaces of the stories it depends on (never their internals) — could rebuild it and pass its tests. The rebuilt internals may legitimately differ; many implementations satisfy one set of contracts.
fields.howToApply: When authoring or revising a story, ask: could someone rebuild this from its spec and contracts plus its upstream stories' public interfaces alone? If the answer needs a neighbour's internals, either name that interface on the upstream story or move the outcome to where it belongs. It is an authoring guideline, not a check.
fields.description: Write a story self-contained enough that a cold agent could rebuild it from its own spec plus its upstream stories' declared interfaces.

fields.why: Without a direction rule, dependency gets decided by intuition, and one outcome counted in two stories reads as a mutual dependency (0.2's ci-cd/studio-cloud trap, where 'keep the studio fresh' belonged to ci-cd alone). With one package per story, a story cycle is a package import cycle, which is unbuildable and untestable in isolation.
fields.title: Cross-story dependency direction and the no-cycle rule
fields.statement: Story A depends on story B if and only if A needs B's delivered outcome, consumed through B's declared interface, to deliver and pass its own contracts. Ask it both ways for any pair: the 'yes' gives the edge direction, and 'yes' both ways is a cycle. A cycle is a modelling error to resolve, never an edge to tolerate.
fields.howToApply: If a capability consumes a sibling story's interface, the whole story depends on that sibling — record it; do not drop a real edge because it feels foundational. A 'trunk' is not declared; it is a root many stories depend on. A story everything ships through (CI) is a process fact, not a dependency. To break a cycle, cheapest first: (1) give the double-counted outcome to ONE story; (2) extract a shared upstream both depend on; (3) if the coupling is real both ways but only one way is an import, invert it — the lower story owns a seam (a callback or extension point) and the higher one plugs in at the composition root; (4) merge the stories only if they are genuinely one journey.
fields.description: A story depends on another only when it needs that story's delivered outcome to deliver its own; the story graph is acyclic, and an apparent cycle is fixed by re-allocating the double-counted outcome.

fields.why: An observability surface exists to expose what the operator must see and judge; a de-noise that drops a signal erases exactly that, invisibly — the picture looks clean because the thing you needed is gone. In 0.2 a generic 'uses a shared island' stamp kept THAT a coupling existed but lost WHICH one and its direction, hiding an architecturally important studio→cli dependency behind something that looked routine.
fields.title: De-noising promotes a signal, never drops it
fields.statement: When you de-noise a crowded view, demote each crowding element to a low-salience rendering; never remove a real signal. Lowering a real coupling's or state's salience is de-noise; making it unrecoverable from the picture — or flattening distinct things into one generic badge — is a drop, and a drop is information loss.
fields.howToApply: Before removing anything to reduce clutter, ask: is this a signal (a real coupling, a real state) or decoration? Re-render signals at lower volume with identity and direction preserved, rather than summarising them away. Drop only genuine decoration. Whether a surfaced coupling is wrong stays the operator's read; the view keeps it visible, it does not judge it.
fields.description: When a dense observability view is de-noised, every real signal is kept at lower salience — a stamp, a thin line, a badge — never deleted.

fields.why: Across 82 of the owner's sessions, every explicit decision grant widened a resource ('as many agents as needed') and none named a standard — so the resource grant is the only thing present that looks like permission, and it gets read as one. Meanwhile a domain the library is silent on routes to the owner every time by design, so more escalation rules cannot help; only the library ceasing to be silent does.
fields.title: Decide against a standard, not a budget
fields.statement: A session may decide in the owner's stead only against a WRITTEN standard — a principle, guardrail, decision or process another reader could hold the call up to. A spend, turn or agent budget bounds what a decision may COST and says nothing about whether it is RIGHT. A domain that produces the same escalation repeatedly is reporting a missing standard; writing it is part of the work.
fields.howToApply: Before deciding for the owner, name what you would be checked against. If the honest answer is 'I was under budget', you have a cost bound, not a license. Test: had the grant been half the size, would the decision's content differ? When the same escalation arrives twice, treat it as a finding: if the decision will recur, write the standard (usually a principle) as part of the work; if not, decide it, record both sides, move on. When you do escalate a recurring fork, ask for the standard along with the instance. This never moves a call the owner owns (irreversible, outward-facing, value-laden) and never substitutes for CI or an owner attestation.
fields.description: What licenses a session to decide in the owner's stead is a written standard it can be checked against, never a spend, turn or agent budget; a recurring escalation signals a missing standard.

fields.why: A shallow module adds names, invariants and parameters to learn without hiding real complexity, so the boundary costs more than it saves. A deep module lets callers see one concept and trust it.
fields.title: Deep modules
fields.statement: A module's interface is a cost paid by every caller, so pay it only when the functionality it hides justifies it. Prefer deep modules (small surface, large hidden work) over shallow ones (wide surface, little hidden).
fields.howToApply: Run the deletion test: imagine deleting the module. If complexity vanishes, it was a pass-through and the boundary is not earning its keep. If complexity reappears across several callers, keep it. Apply this when deciding what a story's package exports and when tempted to add a thin wrapper layer. (Ousterhout, via Matt Pocock.)
fields.description: An interface is a cost every caller pays; draw a boundary only where the functionality it hides justifies that cost.

fields.why: Filing the bug as a new unit splits ownership of one behaviour between the unit that owns it and the unit that records its defect, and breaks the contract-to-evidence chain on the original capability.
fields.title: Defects amend the owning capability
fields.statement: When a defect violates a capability's contract, reopen work on that owning capability and fix it under its existing contract, rather than spawning a new story, capability or arc to hold the bug.
fields.howToApply: Find the capability whose contract the defect breaks. Record the fix as an increment against that capability (claim the capability through the agent link), add or tighten the test that protects the violated behaviour, and fix it there. You give up a new unit's clean slate in exchange for one accountable owner per behaviour.
fields.description: A defect is fixed under the capability whose contract it violates, not filed as a new unit.

fields.why: The orchestrating session's context is the most expensive real estate: every turn re-bills the whole history. Exploration is high-volume and single-use. Trace mining in 0.2 (about 10.6B billed tokens) found raw exploration left in a main session was re-billed 50-65 times versus about 26 times in a half-size subagent context that dies at digest-return, an estimated 14% of all tokens and the largest single saving found.
fields.title: Delegate exploration to digest-returning subagents
fields.statement: When work needs roughly three or more consecutive Read/Grep/Glob turns, or a broad "find where X lives / sweep many files" question, delegate it to a read-only explorer subagent and ask for a DIGEST: conclusions plus file:line pointers. A single targeted lookup where the file or symbol is already known stays inline.
fields.howToApply: Before reading, ask: will this take three or more search/read turns, or is it a sweep? If yes, spawn an explorer subagent and request a digest, not a dump. If no, do it inline. When the digest returns and you need a specific pointer, read that exact span inline. This decides WHERE exploration runs; how the explorer behaves is exploration-principles.
fields.description: Multi-step or broad exploration runs in a read-only subagent that returns conclusions plus file:line pointers, not raw file contents in the main session.

fields.why: It is easy to author "extend the code so the doc holds" or "tighten the invariant" on top of a doc claim a recent finding already showed false. That move rests on a phantom premise.
fields.title: Implementation outranks the doc
fields.statement: Implementation is ground truth and doc text (decision, definition, principle, spec, note) is a hypothesis about it. When a finding shows a doc claim disagrees with the code, the gap is the load-bearing surface; do not build the next move on the doc claim.
fields.howToApply: If a recent investigation named a doc-vs-code gap AND your pending move cites that same doc as load-bearing, stop and surface the gap: the doc, its exact claim, the observed behaviour, and one question - correct the doc or extend the code? Usually the doc is corrected in the library and the downstream move dissolves; code extension is its own bounded unit. If no gap has been named yet, prose-names-a-set-it-never-checked is the proactive complement.
fields.description: Code is ground truth; when a doc claim and the code disagree, the gap itself is what must be surfaced, not built on.

fields.title: Edit-first curation
fields.problem: Duplicate notes split authority — a reader does not know which to trust — and a fresh note severs the history and evidence already attached to the original. In 0.2 an adjudicator routed a rule to a brand-new principle because it searched only the principle/guardrail/pattern kinds, while a process note already stated the rule more fully; a narrow sweep and a full one both read afterwards as 'searched, nothing found'.
fields.approach: Search before you write (`storytree library search "<terms>"`, or the agent link's search_notes) across all guidance-bearing kinds — principle, guardrail, pattern, process, definition — since a rule can live completely in a process or a definition. Edit the closest match by default (`storytree library edit`). If you still write a new note, justify it in the note or PR: the terms searched, the kinds covered, the closest existing note, and why editing it was wrong. An unnamed sweep is unfalsifiable.
fields.statement: Edit is the default; authoring a new note is the justified exception, taken only after searching every guidance-bearing kind for what already exists and naming that search.
fields.tradeoffs: Up-front search and the effort of bending an existing note to fit, against split authority and a broken evidence chain downstream. A new note is faster in the moment and leaves readers unsure which is canonical.
fields.description: Editing the closest existing note is the default; writing a new one is the justified exception, taken only after a named search.

fields.why: Eventual consistency is an escalation policy, not an ownership transfer: it needs a named convergence mechanism. "The owner will catch it in a retro" names a category, not an instrument, and can never be seen to fail. Every gradient (deferring is free now, its cost lands on a later session) pushes toward the unnamed deferral, so naming is the only counterweight.
fields.title: Escalate inline, or on a named signal
fields.statement: Once owner-fork-bar says a decision is the owner's, it reaches the owner one of exactly two ways: INLINE before the work lands, or on the signal of a NAMED instrument that will fire on its own. Deferring without naming the detector is not eventual consistency but silent divergence. This decides only WHEN the owner hears, never WHO owns the call.
fields.howToApply: Runs after owner-fork-bar. (1) Would deciding now blind an instrument the owner relies on? Then escalate inline. (2) Can you name a concrete instrument (a specific failing test or CI check, an open question on the arc, a scheduled measurement) and does the damage stay bounded across its real latency? Then you may defer - and say in the debrief which instrument and roughly when. (3) Cannot name one? Escalate inline, or build the instrument as part of the work. Unnameable means inline. When escalating, raise an open question on the owning arc; chat alone reaches no surface.
fields.description: An owner decision reaches the owner either before it lands or on a named instrument's signal, never on nothing.

fields.rule: Three triggers: (1) the work is outside your role or authority; (2) no process covers it and a library search did not surface one; (3) a missing capability blocks you. On any of them, STOP and name the trigger and the reason in your return message. Do not invent a process, do not produce a green that proves nothing, do not drop the work quietly. Trigger (3) is a claim about the world, so re-check it before handing it up: `git fetch origin` and look at `origin/main` — once a whole orientation declared a unit blocked on a prerequisite that had landed, with seven other PRs, while it was orienting. The same applies one rung higher, session to owner: a stale block spends the owner's time on a question that already answered itself.
fields.title: Escalate up when blocked or out of scope
fields.statement: A specialist never improvises a process, force-fits a hollow proof, or silently skips work — it stops and hands the situation up to the session that spawned it.
fields.enforcedBy: Discipline, carried in each role's own guidance. Nothing mechanical can detect "should have escalated but didn't", or refetch on your behalf.
fields.description: A spawned specialist that hits work outside its role, with no process, or blocked by a missing capability stops and hands it up with the reason.
fields.failureMode: A thin-prompted specialist improvises an unsanctioned process, fakes a proof, or drops the work, and the session never learns the unit stalled or that a capability is missing.

fields.why: The decode is silent and selective, so it corrupts instruments rather than failing commands: in 0.2 a heredoc turned a word-boundary regex into a backspace so a probe reported "28 of 28 uncovered" into an accepted decision; a NUL in a template literal made a source file binary to grep so a declared symbol read as absent; a PowerShell backtick stored "cquired" in the live library. Once the byte is on disk, a further Edit re-emits it and one-liner repairs are refused or wrong.
fields.title: An escape sequence in a tool argument becomes a real byte
fields.statement: Never type an escape sequence into a tool-call argument and expect it to survive as text. Edit/Write strings, Bash heredocs, sed, PowerShell backticks and perl replacements all decode, consume or reinterpret escapes, usually silently. Keep tool-call strings pure printable ASCII and construct control characters at runtime.
fields.howToApply: In code and tests, build control characters with String.fromCharCode and concatenate. Author scripts containing regex escapes as FILES with the Write tool, then run them; never heredoc, sed -i, or node -e one-liners. Pass long prose to storytree through a file argument written with Write; never put backticked prose in a double-quoted PowerShell argument. Verify: grep -a over the file ("Binary file matches" is the tell) and read store fields back. If a byte is already on disk, repair it with a helper file that constructs the byte at runtime, then check with cat -A.
fields.description: Tool-call channels decode escapes before text lands, so keep tool-call strings printable ASCII and build control characters at runtime.

fields.title: An example carries its discriminator
fields.problem: Examples that show only the correct action let an agent pattern-match the incidentals instead of the principle, so it fails on the cases the example did not enumerate and may copy its irrelevant specifics. A worked case is high-attention space spent without buying discriminatory power.
fields.approach: Use the shape input -> action -> rationale, where the rationale states why A and not B. Reserve examples for the judgement calls agents actually miss; spend attention where discriminatory power is highest. The rationale line, not the action, is the part that transfers.
fields.statement: A worked example earns its place only when it carries the discriminating rationale — why the shown move is right and the tempting alternative is wrong. An example without that rationale teaches surface mimicry, not the rule.
fields.tradeoffs: The effort of stating the discriminator precisely, against examples that look instructive but do not transfer — and against burning attention on cases the agent already gets right.
fields.description: A worked example in guidance must include the rationale naming why this move beats the tempting alternative; without it the example is decoration.

fields.why: Exploration feeds a decision. Its risks are over-reading (burning the context budget on exhaustive cataloguing), over-reaching (analysing a surface another agent owns) and quietly mutating what was meant only to be read.
fields.title: Exploration principles
fields.statement: When exploring code or the library to inform a decision, discover patterns rather than enumerate files, load the minimum context for the scope, stay independent of other explorers, and never modify anything.
fields.howToApply: Use glob/search to learn structure and sample representative files instead of reading everything. Stay inside the assigned scope; note, do not analyse, neighbouring surfaces. Report the patterns that matter, flag risks and unknowns explicitly, and return a self-contained result with concrete file:line pointers. Use read-only tools only. If the material genuinely exceeds one context, split it across several explorers rather than reading it all at once.
fields.description: Exploration is read-only reconnaissance: discover patterns over enumerating files, stay context-minimal, stay in scope, never mutate.

fields.steps:
1. Ask in order, writing each answer into the reason: (1) does the evidence support the claim, not merely exist? (a real cold-start log once "supported" a rule it actually contradicted); (2) would a fresh agent re-derive this from the library anyway? -> nothing; (3) what is the closest existing note, and why is editing it not enough?; (4) is it stateless (true beyond this moment)? uncertain stays open; (5) name the future situation where an agent acts differently; (6) has it recurred, or is it structurally certain to?; (7) what is the cheapest fix - a code or tool fence beats prose an agent must remember.
2. Route: nothing (archive with the reason; recurrence re-opens it) / edit-existing / principle or guardrail / process / definition / decision (drafted as PROPOSED - that is the owner escalation; a batch adjudication is never owner-directed, so never born accepted) / tool (find the arc that owns the remedy - folding into an existing arc is the default - and park an increment naming this item; if the fix already landed, record that instead of parking false work).
3. Match verification to blast radius: routes that render into every future session's guidance (edit-existing, principle, guardrail) need the friction's factual claims independently verified against live sources before anything is written.
4. A decision route first surveys the load-bearing decisions it touches; a contradiction with one halts as an owner question, never drafted around.
5. Stop at routing. The per-route authors execute; the owner ratifies a friction-born decision.
6. A graduated rule is not sacred: new evidence contradicting it is fresh friction, not non-adherence.
fields.title: Friction adjudication
fields.trigger: The pre-merge librarian pass (or a dedicated adjudicator) reaches an open friction item at least one session old and filed by ANOTHER branch - the filer never adjudicates its own item. Drain a few of the oldest per pass, never the whole list.
fields.surfaces: Friction records and their comments, memory candidates and the decision log in the library; `storytree friction` for capture; arcs and increments for the tool route; guidance notes for the rendering routes.
fields.statement: A friction item is drained by answering seven ordered questions and recording the answers as its routing reason, then taking exactly one route: nothing, edit an existing note, a new principle or guardrail, a process, a definition, a decision, or a tool fix parked on the arc that owns it. The first question - does the evidence SUPPORT the claim, not merely exist - is the anchor. Worth is judged, never counted: no count or age decides what graduates.
fields.description: How a friction item is judged and routed: the ordered seven-question gate, then one route, with verification matched to how widely the result will be read.
fields.failureModes:
- Evidence that exists taken as evidence that supports.
- Skipping verification on a guidance-rendering route: a confabulated lesson then self-reinforces in every session.
- A friction-born decision born accepted, forging the owner's ratification.
- Draining the whole list per merge: parallel passes clobber the same notes.
- Adjudicating your own item.
- Archiving as "nothing" just to shrink the queue - the loop performs instead of learning.
- A tool remedy left homeless instead of parked on the arc that will carry it.

fields.why: A session retro is self-report, and a model will manufacture plausible lessons on demand. The specific failure is confabulation atop real evidence: in 0.2 a genuine cold-start log was attached to "always start the DB first", a lesson the log did not support and a standing decision contradicted. A check that evidence merely EXISTS waves that through, and a durable tier admitted by judgment alone rots (a Mem0 audit found 97.8% of 10,134 model-gated entries were junk).
fields.title: Friction earns durable guidance by supporting evidence, not by being reported
fields.statement: Before a friction item's lesson graduates into a principle, guardrail, pattern or process, the cited evidence must SUPPORT the stated lesson - a real command, log or PR is necessary but never sufficient. The lesson must also be irreducible: not reconstructible from today's library, better as an edit to the closest existing note than a new one, stateless, discriminating (it names a future situation where an agent acts differently), recurring or certain to recur, and not better fixed by code. The verdict is a judgment in prose, never a score.
fields.howToApply: When adjudicating a friction item, first trace each citation to the claim: does it substantiate the lesson, or just sit beside it? Fails here even if real. Then apply the rest of the floor: reconstructible means nothing to graduate; prefer editing the nearest note; withhold when unsure; a one-off waits for reinforcement; prefer a tool or code fence over prose to remember. Record the verdict and its reasons on the friction item. The trade is accepted: real but singly-observed signal waits, so the library stays trustworthy.
fields.description: A friction item graduates into guidance only when its evidence actually supports the lesson and the lesson is not already reconstructible; worth is judged, never counted.

fields.title: When a term is in question, the definition note wins
fields.problem: With several layers (packages, CLI, desktop app, decisions, generated guidance) speaking the same vocabulary, a contested term drifts to mean different things in different places unless one source is named authoritative. 0.2 retired its hand-kept glossary file for exactly this reason: it was a second copy that drifted.
fields.approach: Use terms as the definition notes define them, looked up just-in-time (`storytree library read <term>`, or search_notes through the agent link) rather than pre-read. When prose elsewhere disagrees, the definition wins; fix the other prose, or if the definition is wrong, edit the definition (and its decision) rather than redefining locally. Do not keep a glossary file beside the library.
fields.statement: When a term's meaning is in question, the library's `definition` note for it is authoritative — it wins over code comments, README prose, generated guidance and memory — and the reasoning lives in the decision it cites.
fields.tradeoffs: Local freedom to redefine a word, against a single vocabulary every layer shares when it matters.
fields.description: The library's definition notes are the authoritative vocabulary every layer speaks; when a term's meaning is contested, the definition wins.

fields.why: Agents do not weight caps, repetition or urgent language the way a skimming human might; emphasis adds noise without raising compliance. Ignored guidance is almost always structural: the instruction is absent at the decision point, lacks a concrete example, or lacks a constraint that removes the ambiguity.
fields.title: Guidance quality: structure over emphasis
fields.statement: When guidance is not being followed, fix its structure - add the missing path, signpost, fence or offload - rather than adding emphasis.
fields.howToApply: Reach for: a PATH (a concrete step placed where it is needed), a SIGNPOST (a concrete example, ideally a link to a real one), a FENCE (a constraint that makes the wrong move structurally hard or measurable), or an OFFLOAD (move a deterministic, error-prone step into code or the CLI). Avoid caps, repetition, escalating urgency on already-ignored guidance, and negative framing with no positive alternative ("writes land only in the declared scope" beats "do not write outside the scope"). Use emphasis only after structure has genuinely failed.
fields.description: Fix unfollowed guidance with structure (path, signpost, fence, offload), not emphasis (caps, repetition, strong language).

fields.rule: Inner loop: building one unit to green — automatable. Outer loop: design forks, accepting how work is split, retrying, amending or abandoning a unit, anything irreversible or outward-facing, anything the library does not settle — the owner's. When you reach one, raise an open question on the owning arc (`storytree question ...`) with enough context to answer it cold, land whatever is already green, release your claims, and stop; do not sit waiting. When the owner answers, record the decision and settle the question with the answer. Standing delegation the owner already gave is not an owner fork — do not re-ask it.
fields.title: The owner owns the outer loop
fields.statement: An agent never takes an owner-level decision on its own; it raises the question on the arc and lands what it can.
fields.enforcedBy: Discipline, plus branch protection: a change reaches main only through a PR that CI verifies, so no agent path merges unverified work. Nothing mechanical stops an agent deciding a fork itself.
fields.description: Driving a unit to green is the agent's job; owner-level calls — design forks, how work is split, abandoning work, irreversible or outward actions — are the owner's.
fields.failureMode: An agent decides a fork, accepts its own decomposition, or abandons work unilaterally, removing the owner's judgment from the loop he owns; or an escalation lives only in chat and reaches no surface.

fields.why: Fragmenting one journey across stories scatters its proof: no single story's tests walk the consumer's actual end-to-end path, and the seams between fragments are where unproven behaviour hides. Since each story owns one package, over-splitting also multiplies package boundaries. "Consumer" generalises "user" on purpose: a substrate story such as the library still has a journey (an agent or contributor), so it is inside this rule, never an exception.
fields.title: The journey principle
fields.statement: A story encompasses one complete consumer journey, where the consumer may be a person, an agent, or another story. If finishing story A naturally leads that consumer to need story B, they are the same journey and likely the same story.
fields.howToApply: Default: do not split. For any proposed story boundary ask: would the consumer, on finishing the first story, immediately need the second to get value? If yes, it is one story. A story feeling like "trunk" or "substrate" is never a reason to split or exempt it; that is just the shape of something many stories depend on.
fields.description: A story covers one complete consumer journey; if finishing A naturally leads the consumer to need B, they are the same story.

fields.steps:
1. Name the escape as inputs -> wrong outcome that reached main. "Nothing went wrong yet but it could" is usually a no.
2. Find the real recorded history the check would have read (a ledger, event rows, CI runs). Do not construct a sample - a series you build answers about your imagination.
3. Replay it through the shipped predicate, prefix by prefix - a check reads the state at one run, not the end state.
4. Count fires and, separately, catches: did any change get made because of a verdict?
5. Check cadence: a red that needs more history than the time between merges passes green through the escape and then blocks every unrelated merge.
6. Check the subject: machine-local state (a home directory, a local cache) does not exist in CI and is not shipped behaviour.
7. Do not settle for a non-blocking "report" row that prints PASS or SKIP while the thing is broken - a signal that deserves a voice goes on a report or an on-demand command (like `pnpm test-ratio`).
8. Record the verdict either way, and sweep every place that described the check as coming.
fields.title: Justify a new check
fields.trigger: Anyone proposes a new CI step, an always-run test or check, or flips a report to blocking - including a sentence in a decision, increment or docstring calling such a check "the natural follow-up", which the next session will read as a task.
fields.surfaces: CI workflow and `pnpm test` always-run units; recorded history (library events, CI run history); a decision note for a justified check.
fields.statement: A check that runs on every PR or every `pnpm test` is a cost every merge pays. It earns its place only by a concrete escape - inputs that led, or would lead, to a wrong outcome on main - shown by running its own predicate over the real recorded history. A zero over a real window is a refusal, not a "not yet".
fields.description: Before adding a check every change pays for, show a real escape it would have caught - by replaying recorded history through its own predicate, not by argument.
fields.failureModes:
- A plausible, tested fence nobody needed: in 0.2 sixteen gate rungs were retired having enforced nothing a merge needed, and roughly three in four judgment-shaped blockers were wrong about the specific defect.
- A refused check left described as pending, then re-derived from scratch within days.
- A slow-cadence red that blocks every unrelated merge.

fields.why: An ungranted tool is a wall an agent cannot rationalise past; an over-granted one is authority the role's prose must then police. The grant IS the boundary, so bloat in it is bloat in the agent's authority.
fields.title: Least-authority tool grants
fields.statement: An agent role's tools list only the tools a named workflow step actually uses; every grant names the step that demands it, and silent widening is a defect.
fields.howToApply: When authoring or auditing an agent role note, walk its workflow steps and map each tool to the step that uses it. A tool with no step is removed; a step with no tool is an escalation. Widening a grant requires naming the new step that needs the new tool.
fields.description: Grant an agent role only the tools a named workflow step uses; every grant names the step that demands it.

fields.why: Automatic framing optimises for containment and is silent on legibility, so a collapsed render passes any bounds-based check. In 0.2 a camera change shrank the forest map's content about 28x inside an unchanged frame; every island was still drawn in the right colour and tests stayed green, but status could no longer be read, and a blind reviewer passed it because no standard said otherwise. The surface is an observability layer: unreadable at rest, it is a picture of one.
fields.title: Legible at the resting view
fields.statement: A visual surface's PRIMARY OBJECTS - fixed by what the surface is for, never chosen by whoever is judging it - must be distinguishable at its RESTING VIEW, before any zoom, pan or filter. Containing the content is not presenting it. And where an element carries meaning (status, kind, health), no appearance change may leave that meaning unreadable at rest, including a change that never meant to touch it.
fields.howToApply: Measure two numbers from one capture: the fraction of the frame the content occupies, and whether the smallest primary object still shows the feature that distinguishes it (status tint, shape, label). For any appearance change (camera, scale, palette), list the signals the surface encodes and check each is still distinguishable after the change - present is not enough. Primacy belongs to the surface's owner; if your verdict turns on your own guess of what is primary, that is a design question for the owner. Secondary content one visible control away is on-demand, not absent, but a surface may not hide its own primary objects behind a control. If a composition you want costs a signal, state the trade and escalate it; do not absorb it.
fields.description: A visual surface's primary objects, and the meaning they carry, must be distinguishable at the view a reader arrives at, before any zoom or pan.

fields.steps:
1. Search first: `storytree library search <words>`, `storytree library links <note>`, `storytree library list <kind>`. Edit the closest existing note; making a new one needs a reason why an edit was wrong. Duplicates split authority and nobody knows which copy is canonical.
2. Write: `storytree library edit <id> --<field> <value|@file>` or `storytree library new <kind> --<field> <value|@file> ...`. The library validates every write and refuses a bad record with its own message. Arcs, increments, questions, decisions, friction and re-steers have their own verbs - use them.
3. Long or multi-line text goes through `@file`, never inline in the shell: shells cut values at inner quotes and exit 0 (PowerShell stored 30 of 65 characters once).
4. A field write REPLACES the field. To add to a long field, start the file from the CURRENT stored text (read the record) and append - never write only the new section, which silently discards the rest (0.2 lost ~1,000 unrecoverable characters of a body this way). Never capture a value with a shell `>` redirect under `pnpm`: the run banner lands as the field's first bytes.
5. Edited a guidance note (agent role, principle, guardrail, pattern, process, definition)? Run `pnpm build:guidance`, commit the regenerated files, and confirm `pnpm check:guidance` is green - generated files are never hand-edited.
6. After a write that matters, `storytree library history <id>` shows what actually landed; a loss is visible there and nowhere in the current state.
7. Keep two sessions off the same record: the same field edited twice is last-write-wins with no warning.
fields.title: Library edit ceremony
fields.trigger: A session needs to create, edit or retire a library record rather than read one. Reads need no ceremony.
fields.surfaces: The project's local Postgres library via `storytree library` (search, links, list, read, new, edit, history) and the agent link's write tools; generated guidance files via `pnpm build:guidance`.
fields.statement: The library is the one edit surface: no committed file mirrors it, and files are generated from it. Change it only through the `storytree` CLI (or the agent link's write tools) - search before writing, edit the closest existing note by default, and carry long text through a file.
fields.description: How a session changes library state: search first, write through `storytree library`, carry long text in files, regenerate guidance after guidance edits.
fields.failureModes:
- Hand-editing a generated guidance file, or editing a note and not regenerating: the next session reads stale guidance.
- Retyping a field out of a rendered view: the view is a projection and the change lands as a silent rewrite.
- Writing only the new section to a long field (a replace read as an append).
- Skipping the search: a second note on the same subject.
- Two sessions editing the same field: the earlier edit vanishes.
fields.verification: The library validates each write. `pnpm check:guidance` catches a guidance edit that was never regenerated. Nothing detects a lost tail or a clobbered field except `library history`.

fields.rule: Write library content through the validated path: `storytree library new|edit`, `storytree adr push`, the `arc` and `question` verbs, or the agent link's `write_note` and plan tools. Never hand-edit a generated file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, agent files): edit the library entry and run `pnpm build:guidance`. Never add a second copy of knowledge that belongs in the library — a committed mirror, a loose prose doc in the repo, a local notes file; durable knowledge is a typed note, and the README is the only standalone narrative doc. Two sessions editing different entries never contend; two editing the same field are last-write-wins, so reconcile forward from the other's text.
fields.title: The library is the edit surface
fields.statement: Every note, decision, arc and role is written through the library's write path — there is one copy, and every generated file is a projection of it.
fields.enforcedBy: The library's own write refusals (every write is validated at its boundary), and `pnpm check:guidance`, which fails when a generated file drifts from the library.
fields.description: Library content is edited only through the library's own validated write path; generated files are regenerated from it, never hand-edited.
fields.failureMode: Knowledge forks: a hand-edited projection or a loose doc disagrees with the library, readers cannot tell which is canonical, and a regeneration or reload silently reverts someone's edit — 0.2 lost parallel sessions' edits to a bulk seed reload before it deleted the seed.

fields.why: A human where a machine would do becomes the queue: work waits on an evening and the backlog outgrows the human. It teaches sessions to escalate by reflex, and an unexercised human gate degrades into a rubber stamp that still looks like a control. The no-self-signing rule is about independence, not species. Owner, 2026-08-21: models have improved and human-in-the-loop as a requirement is no longer something to push.
fields.title: Machine in the loop is the default; a human is the exception
fields.statement: A human is required in a loop ONLY when the judgment is TASTE (an aesthetic or owner value call, or accepting risk on work the system did not produce) or when MODELS ARE NOT YET CAPABLE of making it. Everything else is machine in the loop. No model signs off its own output, but that is satisfied by INDEPENDENCE - a separate session, a separate agent, a judge panel, CI - never by inserting a person.
fields.howToApply: Before requiring a human anywhere (an approval, a gate, a hand-back), ask in order: (1) Is it taste? Then human, permanently. (2) If not, are models genuinely incapable today - not unharnessed, not expensive, not slow? A missing harness is a build task and cost is never a basis. If you rest a requirement on incapability, say so and say what would retire it. Otherwise it is machine: have a different session or agent judge than authored, or let CI observe, and record which independence you relied on. Before escalating at all, check whether the owner already delegated this class of decision.
fields.description: Require a human only for taste or a judgment models cannot yet make; independence, not a person, is what keeps a verdict honest.

fields.why: Session cost is input-side: every turn re-bills the whole carried context. A poll tick re-reads everything to learn one bit that is almost always "not yet", so its price scales with context size times wait length, and it bites late in long sessions, right before landing. Measured in 0.2 over ten sessions: 10% of session spend was pure polling. A hand-written loop also needs a hand-written terminal condition, which tends to be wrong in the confident direction.
fields.title: Mechanical waiting never pays context rent
fields.statement: Waiting for a MACHINE - a CI run, a long test run, an install, a migration - is dispatched and notified, never polled in a loop. Run it in the background and let its completion re-enter you, or take ONE bounded wait on a stated condition. Never a sleep-and-re-read loop.
fields.howToApply: Before any wait, ask what ends it. A machine: background it and let the runtime notify you, then do other work. A person: that is not a wait at all - raise the open question and land. Never let a foreground call be the only thing holding long work; foreground timeouts are capped and can clamp silently. A bounded wait's condition must be the real terminal predicate - the process exit status - not a log line that also appears mid-run or a word that occurs in test names. Do not background something you need on the very next line, or something shorter than the dispatch overhead. A dispatched result nobody read is unverified, not passed.
fields.description: Wait for a machine by dispatching it and being notified, never by a sleep-and-re-read loop that re-bills the whole context to learn "not yet".

fields.steps:
1. Verify over the FINAL tree: `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test` (plus `pnpm check:guidance` if you edited guidance notes). Any edit after a green - a librarian fix, a memory, a doc tweak - stales it; re-run before committing.
2. Finish the pre-merge librarian pass BEFORE opening the PR (a green PR automerges within minutes, so the PR is the last moment you control).
3. Commit on the session branch (never on main), push, `gh pr create` as a non-draft PR. Then stop. Never `gh pr merge` yourself: the automerge job merges exactly the commit verify passed; a hand merge was how 0.2 landed unverified work.
4. To hold a PR, mark it draft or add the `hold` label. A hold is temporary: flip it back the moment the unit is green. PRs merge as true merge commits, never squashed.
5. Watch CI (`gh pr checks <n>`). CI tests the merge with main, so a local green can still go red: first suspect a stale branch - merge origin/main, `pnpm install`, re-verify, push.
6. Closing leg, once the merge is confirmed, in order: (a) close the increment with its outcome and its PR number (close the existing one; never mint a second), and `land` each capability whose work finished; (b) `release` any capability or increment claim you still hold through the agent link (a merge ends the claims on its branch; release anything taken on another branch); (c) leave the worktree clean and no background work running; (d) debrief the owner in two slots - WHAT LANDED (PR numbers plus a plain-language paragraph of what now works) and SAFE TO CLOSE (a literal yes or no: PRs merged, tree clean, claims released). Every other concern becomes an object - a fix on its own PR, an increment on the arc, or an open question - not a debrief paragraph.
7. Blocked mid-unit: land what is genuinely green, write the residue onto the OPEN increment (what was tried, done, not done, what the owner was asked, how to resume), raise the question on the arc and make the increment wait on it, release claims, end. A refused claim (held by another live session, or waiting on other work) is the same landing minus the question: nobody queues, so pick other work - a claim conflict is never an owner question.
8. Continue or go inert. The merged branch is dead: new code goes in a fresh worktree from freshly fetched origin/main. Continuing is the DEFAULT. Stop only for one of four reasons, named in the debrief: (a) OWNER GATE - the next work needs a look, decision or spend only the owner can give, authored as a question on the arc; (b) CONTEXT MARK - your harness reports your own window is near its limit (on Claude: take no new unit past ~700K, hand over at ~850K); (c) HARD END - a workstream fork or visibly degraded context; (d) EMPTY WORKLIST - nothing ready you may claim. Draining one arc is not a reason: pick the next work from `storytree arc list`. If a real end arrives with ready work left, cut the successor session yourself rather than leaving the owner a click.
fields.title: Merge ceremony
fields.trigger: A unit of work is done and `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm test` pass over the exact tree you are about to commit, with nothing red or WIP in the diff. Run it without being asked: sitting on green work is the failure this exists to stop. Second entry: the session is blocked mid-unit on an owner decision, or its claim on the unit is refused - that is a landing too, not a pause (see step 7).
fields.surfaces: git branch and PR (`gh`); CI workflow (verify on three OSes, automerge job); the library via `storytree` (increment outcome, open questions); agent-link claim tools (`claim`, `land`, `release`) on capabilities and increments.
fields.statement: When a unit is green, commit, push, open a non-draft PR and stop: CI verifies the merge with main on Linux, macOS and Windows and automerges. A session never merges by hand. After the merge, run the closing leg, then keep going unless one of four named reasons stops you.
fields.description: How a green unit lands on main: PR, CI on three systems, automerge; then the closing leg and the continue-or-inert call.
fields.failureModes:
- Manual `gh pr merge`: in 0.2 it landed before CI with no check at all.
- Sitting on green work, or leaving a finished unit in draft: the owner had to keep asking sessions to open or un-draft PRs.
- Red/WIP in a non-draft PR: it automerges the moment it happens to go green.
- Running the librarian pass after opening the PR: automerge beat it and its edits stranded on a dead branch.
- Committing a tree the checks never saw: the post-green edit reaches main with CI as its first check.
- Editing on in the merged worktree: its claims are gone and its next PR is refused.
- Waiting on the owner while holding a claim: the work goes invisible and blocks the next session.
- Going inert with ready work and no named reason (measured: most "safe to close" sessions had landed one PR while the owner kept typing "continue").
fields.verification: Branch protection on main requires `verify`, which passes only when Linux, macOS and Windows all passed against the merge with main; the automerge job skips drafts, `hold` and forks, and merges the exact head commit verify saw. The closing leg and the continue-or-inert call are discipline: nothing checks them.

fields.why: In 0.2 the red side had no volume counterweight: by 2026-09-24 it carried 264k lines of test against 189k of implementation, 782 of 1,014 test files cited decision records and 1,078 assertions checked that something was absent. Tests had become the enforcement arm of the decision log; they failed when wording or files moved, not when the product broke. This is the owner-directed minimal viable TDD rule for 0.3.
fields.title: Minimum test to red: pin the missing behaviour, nothing else
fields.statement: Write the minimum test that goes red for the one product behaviour that is missing. Every test protects a behaviour the product has; a test whose subject is a decision record, a removed feature staying removed, the wording of prose or source, or the shape of the repository is not written.
fields.howToApply: Before writing a test, name in one sentence the product behaviour it protects, as a user would recognise it. If you cannot, do not write it. Pin that behaviour with the fewest tests that go red for its absence, plus the unhappy paths the behaviour itself has. This limits how MANY and about WHAT, never how weak. A regression test for a real incident is a behaviour test: write it and name the incident in its title. When your work passes an existing test that pins an excluded subject, remove it and say why. Tie-break: if the behaviour disappeared, would this test fail? If it fails only when a file, a word or a decision changes, it is out. Do not add test infrastructure without a product behaviour that needs it.
fields.description: Write the minimum test that goes red for a missing product behaviour; no tests whose subject is a decision, a retirement, prose or repo structure.

fields.rule: Every change lands by PR. CI verifies it on Linux, macOS and Windows against the merge with main and automerges it when green; a draft or a `hold` label holds it. Never `gh pr merge` by hand, never `--no-verify`, never weaken or disable a check to get green, never mark a PR ready while it is red or WIP. An owner approval admits work that already passed; it cannot waive the check. If CI is red, read the failure, fix it (first suspect a stale branch: merge `origin/main`), and push.
fields.title: Verification is never bypassed
fields.statement: Never land un-green work: no manual merge, no skipped check, no disabled hook, no red or WIP change on a ready PR.
fields.enforcedBy: CI `verify` on three systems plus branch protection requiring `verify`, and the automerge job that merges only the verified head commit.
fields.description: A change reaches main only through a PR that CI verifies green; no path skips, waives or hand-merges around it.
fields.failureMode: Unproven or broken work reaches main, and a trunk that auto-merges on green stops being trustworthy — storytree 0.1's trunk tolerated knowingly-broken states for throughput.

fields.rule: (1) Never `x as unknown as T`. Use the real thing (a real object, an in-memory store with one method overridden); or narrow the seam to the surface you actually use so a double satisfies it; or `satisfies Partial<X> as X` for an external type a test cannot build. (2) Never annotate a value wider than what you just wrote (`Record<string, unknown>`, `object`, `unknown`, an anonymous shape): use `as const satisfies Record<Union, V>` for a total table, a `ReadonlyMap` for a partial one, a named interface for a known accumulator. (3) Never `...(cond ? { x } : {})`: add the field in an `if`, or use `cond ? base : { ...base, x }` when there are required fields. Also never `Reflect.apply`, `Reflect.get` or `type X = unknown`. When unsure, let `pnpm typecheck` choose the shape.
fields.title: Types stay honest
fields.statement: Write types that say what the value is: one assertion or none, never widen a literal you just wrote, and add optional fields with visible statements.
fields.enforcedBy: Discipline and review. 0.3 has no lint rung (0.2 held these with oxlint rules at error); `pnpm typecheck` in CI catches what honest types expose.
fields.description: Never launder a value past the compiler — `as unknown as T`, a known value annotated wider than it is, or an omission hidden in `...(c ? {x} : {})`.
fields.failureMode: A test passes against a contract its double does not hold, or a typo'd key becomes a silently dropped field — in 0.2 chained assertions hid a store double missing a method behind twenty cases, and a widened record hid 28 attribute stamps an e2e test read back.

fields.rule: A component that cannot be tested without rewriting imports has a design problem, not a testing problem. Add the seam: declare the narrow surface the consumer actually drives (not somebody else's class — that is half a seam, and the double then needs an assertion), pass it in, and give it a real default so no production caller changes. Then test through the seam against a real or in-memory implementation.
fields.title: Never mock a module — give the code a seam
fields.statement: Never replace a module with a module mock; add a seam — a narrow value carrying only what the consumer uses, passed in, with a real default.
fields.enforcedBy: Discipline and review; 0.3 has no lint rung and no module mocks today — keep it at zero.
fields.description: If a test must substitute a collaborator, the code offers a narrow seam with a real default; the module system is never rewritten under test.
fields.failureMode: The subject never runs and the suite is green anyway — in 0.2 a guard test mocked its module so the guard never executed, and deleting the guard clause left every test green.

fields.why: "All tests pass", reported without the verbatim summary line, was falsified by a re-run (the 0.1 f53caac lesson). Paraphrase is where optimism, hallucination and reward-hacking hide; a finding asserted from impression fabricates state, and an "environment / OS / flaky" framing dodges falsification entirely.
fields.title: No claim without evidence
fields.statement: A claim is admissible only with the evidence that proves it: a verbatim runner summary, a citable path and line, a named command and field, a record id. Never a paraphrase, an impression or a guess.
fields.howToApply: Test claims: run the canonical command (pnpm test, pnpm typecheck) on the post-change tree, read its output, quote the final summary line. Findings: each carries evidence naming a real source - path:line, command plus field, or a library record. When the sources are silent, answer "could not determine", never a guess.
