An environment or flaky framing needs evidence: three-run determinism, an authoritative citation, or a search of the workspace for a working idiom first.
fields.description: A claim is admissible only with the evidence that proves it - verbatim output, a path and line, a command and field, a record id - never a paraphrase or impression.

fields.why: storytree 0.3 is an observability layer beside a coding agent; that is its whole job. Observability bolted on afterwards leaves state changes invisible - behaviour happens that the planet and arc surface cannot show - and no later pass can reconstruct what was never recorded. No external trace service sits in the loop.
fields.title: Observability-first
fields.statement: If a state change is not a typed record the app can render, it does not exist - so design the record (the library row, its lifecycle, the event) before the feature that produces it.
fields.howToApply: For every new state change (an increment moving, a claim taken or ended, a question settled, a read by a session), first decide the typed record in the library that captures it, then build the feature that writes it. Test: if this change happened, could the desktop app show it? If not, it does not exist yet.
fields.description: If a state change is not a recorded, typed fact the app can render, it does not exist; design the record before the feature.

fields.why: This is the rendering-side twin of observability-first. Prettiness is not meaning: a form made to look intricate carries no fact, and there is no single value a story's form should map to. Without this rule every new element re-litigates what the look means, elements get overloaded with two facts at once, and the world drifts from a faithful read of signals into decoration nobody can trust.
fields.title: One element per signal
fields.statement: On storytree's visual surfaces (the forest planet of stories), every observed signal renders as its OWN distinct element, and a story's visual complexity emerges from the stack of those elements, never from a single "complexity" score.
fields.howToApply: Keep encoding channels orthogonal: position carries the dependency structure, form is the stack of signal-to-element mappings, and the ground is a deliberately signal-less canvas. For each new observable fact, add a new distinct element; do not overload an existing one or invent a composite reading. Keep each signal-to-element mapping a cleanly factored renderable, but do not build a pluggable abstraction until two or three real uses exist.
fields.description: Each observed signal renders as its own distinct element on the forest planet; complexity emerges from the stack, never from a composite score.

fields.why: A second route splits muscle memory, doubles what must be built, tested and kept in sync (so one path silently rots), and hides the canonical route behind a choice that buys nothing. Owner-directed after a menu duplicated an existing route in 0.2's studio: "there should be one way to do things, and a second pathway needs very strong justification."
fields.title: One way to do things
fields.statement: A surface - app UI, CLI, agent-link tools, library, or workflow - offers exactly ONE pathway to a given capability. A second pathway to the same destination is a defect until a very strong, explicitly stated justification earns it.
fields.howToApply: Before adding a route to a capability that is already reachable, ask whether one exists. If so, default to removing the new one and pointing at the canonical route. A second pathway clears the bar only on a structurally different context of use - an accessibility need, a genuinely different entry surface (e.g. CLI vs agent-link tool for different callers), an offline/online split. Convenience never clears it. When justified, state the justification where the duplicate is introduced so a later reader does not prune it. When in doubt, one way wins.
fields.description: A surface offers one pathway to a capability; a second pathway needs a strong, stated justification.

fields.title: Decompose by testability; delegate the glue
fields.problem: Treating every piece as needing a test force-fits glue into a hollow test that proves nothing, or the glue is silently skipped. The filter that works is 'does this piece have an isolatable red→green test?', NOT package boundaries: one package can hold both an algorithm worth testing and glue that is not, and a testable behaviour can straddle packages. Look/feel work is a separate axis — judged by a human, not tested (see render-and-witness).
fields.approach: 1. Decompose: the testable units carry the behaviour; the rest is integration. 2. Build testable units red→green, sequenced by dependency; cross-package work lands in order across PRs, never as one atomic change that cannot be proven piece by piece. 3. Delegate glue to subagents with an explicit write fence; write no test for it unless a product behaviour needs one. 4. When a piece genuinely needs a test the tooling cannot yet run (a DB-backed or browser proof), raise it as a capability gap rather than faking the test or skipping it.
fields.statement: The orchestrating session's job is to DECOMPOSE work into units, decide per piece whether it protects a product behaviour with an isolatable red→green test, build those test-first in dependency order, and SUPPLEMENT the glue — wiring, config, dependency additions, adapters with nothing worth asserting — through its own subagents, doing it itself only as a last resort.
fields.tradeoffs: Deciding testable-vs-glue per piece and sequencing across PRs is slower than one atomic change, but an atomic cross-package edit cannot be proven unit by unit and a hollow test is worse than none. The standing risk is the orchestrator quietly absorbing glue it should have delegated.
fields.description: Split work by whether each piece has an isolatable behaviour worth a red-green test, not by package; test those pieces, and hand the untestable glue to subagents without faking a proof.

fields.why: Owner attention is the scarcest channel, and a misrouted fork spends it twice: he first reverse-engineers context the agent already had, then makes a call the agent could have made, so the question sits and the work stalls. In 0.2, questions like "which proof command" reached him already carrying an engineering lean. The opposite error - deciding an irreversible or value-laden call alone - removes him from the loop he owns.
fields.title: The owner-fork bar: escalate ownership, not uncertainty
fields.statement: Raise an owner-facing open question only when the DECISION ITSELF is the owner's - irreversible, outward-facing, or value-laden and not settleable from the decision log - never merely because you are unsure. A reversible, internal call with a defensible engineering answer is decided and recorded, not parked.
fields.howToApply: A fork earns an open question iff at least one holds: (1) IRREVERSIBLE or high blast radius (destroys history, deletes or migrates data, costly to undo); (2) OUTWARD-FACING (changes what users or external parties see or depend on); (3) VALUE-LADEN and unsettled (turns on priorities, direction, taste or risk appetite, not an engineering tradeoff). If none hold, pick the defensible option, name both sides of the tradeoff, record it (a decision note if it outlives the unit, otherwise the unit's own notes), and move on. Tells that a fork is below the bar: it carries a stated lean, its rationale is purely engineering, or it cannot be put in one plain sentence without an identifier. The test is ownership, not whether it deserves a decision record.
fields.description: Raise an open question for the owner only when the decision is his - irreversible, outward-facing, or value-laden and unsettled; decide and record a reversible engineering call.

fields.title: Pair the fence with the affordance
fields.problem: Guidance written as a bare affordance over-fires. An agent told only when to reach for a tool has no signal for when to withhold it, so it fires on weak matches; the boundary, if it exists at all, lives in a distant 'when not to' section that drifts out of sync with the grant.
fields.approach: Do not state an affordance without its negative space, and keep the two adjacent. A CLI line, tool grant, or permitted move is incomplete until it names the condition(s) under which the agent must not take it. Well-built tool prompts show the discipline: nearly every 'when to use' carries a paired 'when NOT to use'.
fields.statement: Every affordance granted to an agent — a tool, a command, a permitted move — ships with its matching fence: at least one explicit condition under which the agent should NOT take it, co-located with the grant.
fields.tradeoffs: Brevity — each affordance gets a clause longer — for precision: fewer false fires and a boundary that cannot drift from the thing it bounds. A separate section reads cleaner but rots.
fields.description: When guidance grants a capability, tool, or move, state its boundary — the when-NOT-to — in the same place, not separately.

fields.title: Parallel build-lane fan-out
fields.problem: Sessions default to serial without knowing what they decline, then get fan-out wrong two ways. They quote the build-phase speedup (2.57x in 0.2's one measured three-lane trial) when end-to-end was 1.71x with serial landing, ~2.8x landing concurrently. And they treat file-disjointness as dispatchability, when two conflict classes are invisible to it.
fields.approach: Check width first: usually nothing to fan (in 0.2 only 2 of 22 active arcs held two or more open increments). 1. Screen each candidate: (a) shared state — a lane writing to the library or to generated guidance can red every other lane's checks on files they never touched; run it alone, before or after the code lanes; (b) a real cross-lane edge — the last line of one increment lives in another lane's fence; the lane STOPS and reports rather than reaching across. 2. Vehicle: subagents dispatched in one turn (a fresh session per lane costs ~9x the onboarding). 3. Isolation: prepare each lane's worktree and claim through the agent link first, then hand the lane its path; a harness 'worktree' option that mints its own tree will ignore a path named in the prompt. 4. Brief each lane's write fence explicitly — nothing enforces it. 5. Budget for finishing seams yourself; in 0.2 one line of seam code cost a full extra CI cycle. 6. Land concurrently; the serial tail was a choice. The accepted risk is two disjoint PRs breaking main semantically, caught after merge; in 0.2 it never fired across 80 runs.
fields.statement: An orchestrating session holding two or more genuinely INDEPENDENT ready increments may build them concurrently as about three subagent lanes, each in its own worktree with its own claim, open every green lane's PR as soon as it is green, and then finish the lanes at their seams itself, serially.
fields.tradeoffs: The win is real but modest and n=1; the token premium was 2–10%. Safety is briefed, not enforced. This is for BUILD lanes only — a read-only exploration still goes to one delegate returning a digest, never N parallel readers.
fields.description: When two or more genuinely independent increments are ready, build them as about three subagent lanes in separate claimed worktrees and land their PRs concurrently — after screening for the conflicts file-disjointness cannot see.

fields.why: Notes are read by newcomers and by agents pulling them just in time without the codebase in mind. A bare identifier or a bare decision number is noise to that reader: it costs attention without conferring the power to decide. A note that opens with the decision instead of the stake makes the reader earn the "why should I care" that should have been free.
fields.title: Plain language first
fields.statement: Write every library note and question so a reader who does NOT have the repo loaded grasps the stake in the first sentence and never hits an unexplained internal term.
fields.howToApply: Three observable checks. (1) Stake in sentence one: say what breaks or is blocked, in plain terms, before any identifier. (2) Jargon budget zero: every internal term, code identifier and decision number gets a short gloss or a link on first use. (3) Draw the structure: if the subject is a structure, flow or state machine, include a diagram. Scope: this governs notes and questions. Talking to the OWNER is different - he set the project and needs only the machine vocabulary translated (name things by what they do, lead with the answer or the ask), never the project re-explained; applying newcomer glossing to him reads as padding.
fields.description: Lead with the stake, gloss every internal term and decision number on first use, and draw structural subjects - so a reader without the repo loaded can decide.

fields.steps:
1. Decide whether curation fires (diff + your own library writes). Graduation runs regardless.
2. Graduate: for each memory, friction item or rule this session learned, extract the durable essence (a principle, definition, process) - never the event record ("this PR, this date"), which stays in git and on the arc. Search first (`storytree library search`) and edit the closest existing note before making a new one.
3. Clear what graduated (delete the memory - a kept copy lets sessions read the cache instead of the library). A reviewed memory that will not graduate is kept deliberately, not deleted: machine traps and closed-arc pointers still save real rework.
4. If curation fires: have the librarian keep every accepted decision true in full (correct overtaken prose in place; supersede only on a real re-decision), and settle or retire stale open questions - settle one that got an answer, retire only one that was wrong; retiring an answered question destroys the answer.
5. If you edited guidance notes, regenerate once after all writes land (`pnpm build:guidance`), commit the diff, and re-run `pnpm check:guidance`.
6. Then open the PR. If curation did not fire, say so in the debrief in one line.
fields.title: Pre-merge librarian pass
fields.trigger: Sequence: green unit -> retro (friction / re-steer capture) -> this pass -> open PR -> CI automerges. Graduation: always. Curation fires when the diff against merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) touches generated guidance files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, agent directories), OR this session wrote a decision, agent, principle, guardrail, pattern, process or open-question note. It fails wide: any doubt fires it; skipping means you can SHOW nothing curated was touched.
fields.surfaces: The library via `storytree library` (search, read, edit, new, history) and `storytree decision` / `storytree question`; the librarian package (graduation queue); git diff for the trigger; generated guidance files.
fields.statement: Every landing runs the librarian pass after the unit is green and BEFORE `gh pr create`. It has two halves with different triggers: GRADUATION runs every time, because only this session holds that knowledge and it evaporates when the session ends; CURATION runs when the branch or the session touched curated material, because a stale decision is shared and any later session can repair it. Under pressure the half that gets skipped is graduation - the one nobody else can ever do.
fields.description: After green and before opening the PR: graduate what this session learned (always), and curate the decision log and guidance notes (only when the trigger fires).
fields.failureModes:
- Running it after `gh pr create`: the PR automerged in minutes and the pass edited a dead branch.
- Skipping graduation because curation did not fire - the predictable error under time pressure.
- Guessing "probably nothing to curate" instead of showing it.
- Skipping silently: an unmentioned skip reads as a forgotten one.
- Draining memories that belong to a sibling session still in flight (the memory queue is per machine).
- Regenerating guidance while library writes are still landing: truncated generated text.
fields.verification: Nothing checks that the pass ran, by design: a rung could only read a proxy that is producible without the judgment. `pnpm check:guidance` catches only a missing regeneration.

fields.why: Quoting is free and measuring is not, so an unmeasured estimate propagates verbatim between increments and hardens with each retelling, while slow-growth and owner-fork discipline both reward deferring. Twice on one 0.2 arc the measurement inverted the prose: a coupling risk that deferred the highest-value work for three increments moved the backlog by one item, not the 121 implied; a caveat naming two checks as maybe needing nothing read as settled for four increments, and both needed work.
fields.title: Price the deferral
fields.statement: Prose is not a measurement. Before an untested claim defers work a second time, state its quantity or spend the one probe that settles it - and when writing a hedge, never name instances you have not tested.
fields.howToApply: When a deferral rests on a QUANTITY ("would move a lot", "risks coupling"), require the quantity; spend the probe before carrying the reason into a second increment - it is usually cheaper than another round of quoting. When writing a hedge, keep it about the rule: naming specific instances in an exception clause reads as a verdict on them and later readers route around them untested. Name an instance only with its measurement attached. Distinct from doc-vs-implementation-precedence, where a disagreement is already visible; here nothing looks wrong yet.
fields.description: A blocker that exists only as prose is an untested estimate; state its quantity or spend the probe that settles it before it defers work again.

fields.title: Proof-walkthrough first
fields.problem: A unit authored prose-first can read coherently while being unprovable at its tier: too big for one walkthrough, too small to need one, or placed at a tier whose proof does not fit its behaviour. The defect surfaces only later, when someone tries to prove it and every consumer must be reworked.
fields.approach: Before writing the unit (plan_story / plan_capability / plan_contract, or `storytree library new`), write its proof at the tier's rung: for a STORY, the end-to-end journey a user walks; for a CAPABILITY, the integration test against real collaborators inside the story; for a CONTRACT, the isolated assertion. If you cannot write a coherent walkthrough, re-tier or re-bound before drafting. Never author the walkthrough last, or thicken a thin one with prose to justify a unit that already exists. The proof is a product behaviour worth protecting, not a test of the note itself.
fields.statement: Draft the unit's proof-walkthrough before its prose — the walkthrough is the sizing test that re-tiers a wrong-sized unit before it is authored.
fields.tradeoffs: Walkthrough effort on units that may not survive sizing, against discovering unprovability after the unit is written and cited.
fields.description: Draft a story, capability or contract's proof before its prose; if no coherent proof exists, the unit is the wrong size or tier.

fields.why: A written list carries no marker separating "absent because it does not exist" from "absent because the search did not reach it". In 0.2 it failed both ways: a decision's "every repo root is derived here" inventory named six sites and missed nine, including the one site the decision depended on; a call-site comment claimed a field existed on two option types when it existed on one, and the next increment was scoped as threading work onto a field that did not exist. Both were caught only by a consuming session that re-derived.
fields.title: Prose names a set it never checked
fields.statement: A written list or existence claim - a decision's site inventory, a call-site comment, an increment's "already exists" line - reads as a CHECKED set (nothing missing, everything named real) when its author only wrote down what one search or recollection returned. Re-derive the set against the code before consuming it as a worklist, and scope it to what you actually checked when you write it.
fields.howToApply: CONSUMING a set: ask what single search produced it and whether it would have reached a member spelled differently - the text will not say. Re-derive cheaply: sweep again with an idiom the author plainly did not use (another symbol name, path shape, the declaration rather than the call site), and grep each named member to confirm it exists. Check the set's extent in every dimension it claims. AUTHORING a set: do not write the universal; scope the sentence to the search ("the six sites this grep found"), name a capability as existing only after reading it in code, and when you landed one side of a symmetric pair, describe only that side. If re-deriving surfaces a real code-vs-doc gap, doc-vs-implementation-precedence takes over.
fields.description: A written list or existence claim reads as a checked set even when nobody checked it; re-derive it against the code before using it as a worklist, and scope it to what you searched when writing it.

fields.why: If one actor writes the test, writes the code, runs it and reports the result, the last step is a claim, and nothing has been established. The false greens that actually happen are not forged: they are an agent that honestly believes it succeeded, and a check that exits 0 having asserted nothing (a success flag, a help-text match, a mocked dependency). Both look identical to a real green afterwards. 0.2 rebuilt the author/observer separation as a spine after collapsing to one agent loop removed it; 0.3 keeps the lesson, not the spine.
fields.title: The author of the work is not its only witness
fields.statement: A green is credible only when the party that produced the work is not the only party that observed the result. The author's own report that it passed is an opinion; the proof is a run someone else can repeat and see fail and pass — a test watched going red then green, and CI verifying the merge with main.
fields.howToApply: Ask who ESTABLISHED the fact, not whether it is asserted. Before trusting a new check, ask what input would make it red, produce that input, and watch it fail. Never report 'tests pass' from memory or from a summary — cite the run. Treat CI on the merge with main as the verdict, not your local run. Pin the observable outcome, never a flag or exit code standing in for it.
fields.description: Whoever authored the work does not get to be the only witness that it worked.

fields.title: Pull-based context architecture
fields.problem: Pre-loading a big static brief pays three costs every turn: a context tax (most of it is irrelevant to the step), staleness (a snapshot taken at session start does not reflect later edits), and one-size-fits-all (no step gets context tailored to it). Static instruction is also followed less reliably than context pulled at the step that needs it.
fields.approach: Thin bootstrap: generated guidance (CLAUDE.md, role files) names surfaces and how to reach them, not their contents. Pull on demand: `storytree library search|read|links`, or the agent link's search_notes and record reads, always reading current state. Progressive disclosure: each read points at the next thing worth fetching. Keep briefs to subagents lean: self-contained means complete pointers, not complete payloads. When one context to pull still exceeds the window, decompose instead of summarising lossily: hand a subagent the query, let it filter to the relevant slice in its own window, and take back a cited digest.
fields.statement: Give an agent a thin bootstrap — its role, current objective, and how to fetch more — and let it pull exactly the context its current step needs, from the live source, on demand. Pointers, not payloads.
fields.tradeoffs: A guaranteed-complete upfront snapshot, traded for freshness and a small initial load; the agent makes extra fetches, each reading live state. The cost of the model: a session cannot pull an artifact to decide whether it needs it, so a few judgement calls (whether to fan out, whether to escalate) must live in the thin bootstrap itself.
fields.description: Brief an agent thinly and let it pull fresh context just-in-time, rather than pushing a fat static brief at session start.

fields.why: Escalating feels careful and costs the escalating session nothing; the whole cost lands on the owner's turns, the one resource that does not scale. The owner objected four times in 0.2 ('this feels like you're asking me to stamp something I asked to be done'); in one walkthrough three of seven questions got answers wider than asked. The failing sessions read the clauses accurately — the missing step was asking why the clause existed. Decisions are a record of reasoning, not constitutional law.
fields.title: Read the force a decision answered, not the clause it left behind
fields.statement: When a clause in an accepted decision seems to refuse the work in front of you, its authority is the FORCE it answered — what would go wrong if it were ignored — not the sentence. Name that force and take one of three exits: (A) it still holds here → comply, and say which force; (B) it is dead → the clause is stale prose, and correcting the record is your move; (C) it holds but the clause is a deferral ('not decided here', 'a separate larger decision', 'pending') whose answer somebody can PRODUCE → do the work that answers it. Only a genuine owner call — taste, spend, an irreversible or outward-facing act — goes to the owner.
fields.howToApply: First check it is a CLAUSE, not a wall: a mechanism that refuses (CI, a claim refusal, a failing test) is not this rule's subject — comply. Only an accepted decision's prose is. Step 1: state the force in one sentence without reusing the clause's words; if you can only restate it, you have not found it — read further (Context/Consequences), do not proceed either way. Step 2: take exit A, B or C. For C, look for a precedent that already answered the same question for a neighbour. Test: would the owner answer 'I already told you to do that'? Then it was never his. Whatever exit you take, keep the reason in the record. No exit ever licenses skipping a test, CI or review — this rule can only remove an owner question, never a proof.
fields.description: A decision's clause binds only while the force it answered still holds — read the why before complying or escalating.

fields.why: A test that has never been seen to fail is not evidence — writing the implementation first invites tests shaped to pass vacuously. Watching it go red proves it actually exercises the behaviour.
fields.title: Red-green
fields.statement: A failing (red) test is written and seen to fail before the implementation that turns it green.
fields.howToApply: Write the test, run it and watch it fail for the reason you expect (not a syntax error or an unrelated break), then write the smallest implementation that turns it green. Under minimal viable TDD the test must protect a product behaviour; red-green is how you know it does.
fields.description: Author the failing test before the implementation that turns it green.

fields.why: Restated prose drifts: copy a rule into N bodies and one edit leaves N-1 stale copies, with no reader knowing which is canonical. 0.1 encoded this twice and 0.2 made the library the one copy; 0.3's library is the edit surface and files are generated from it, so a link costs nothing and buys one-edit propagation.
fields.title: Reference, don't restate
fields.statement: A durable rule lives ONCE, as a library note; every consumer — a role, a story, a report, generated guidance — links to it instead of restating it in its own prose.
fields.howToApply: Before writing rule prose into any body, search the library (`storytree library search`). If a note covers it, link it with at most a one-line gloss of why it binds here — and open the note before writing the gloss, because a link riding beside a claim makes the claim look checked. If none does, write the note and link it. A consumer keeps only what is its own: role, boundaries, workflow shape, links. Smell test: if two bodies could share a paragraph, that paragraph is a note.
fields.description: Durable discipline lives once in the library; every other surface links to it rather than copying it.

fields.why: In 0.2 the owner asked what was left on an arc, got an accurate answer, and replied 'can you rephrase with less jargon'; the same facts rephrased got 'this is much easier to read'. Register was the only variable. The owner is not a newcomer — he holds the intent and history better than any session; what he lacks is the machine vocabulary. 'Explain it to a newcomer' produces padding, the worse failure. And ids are how sessions hand off precisely, so this licenses no vagueness in notes.
fields.title: Register follows audience
fields.statement: Choose register by AUDIENCE: compressed and identifier-dense for notes and agent-to-agent handoff; for the OWNER, translate the machine vocabulary — ids, lifecycle terms, decision numbers, internal names — naming each thing by what it DOES, leading with the answer or the ask, and never re-explaining the project he set.
fields.howToApply: A DECISION for the owner: stakes first, every term glossed, options with both sides of each trade-off, a non-binding recommendation, an analogy that says where it breaks, a diagram when the subject is a structure or flow, at most one question — and put it on an open question raised on the arc, not only in chat. A MID-SESSION UPDATE: the answer or ask in sentence one; items named by what they do, id in parentheses at most; decided work split from work needing his call. The LANDING DEBRIEF: what landed (PR numbers + a plain outcome paragraph) and whether the session is safe to close, yes or no. RE-ONBOARDING a cold owner: where things stand, what he needs to know, what you make of it, what you want from him. Offer the analogy or diagram unasked — being asked for one is the failure signal.
fields.description: Translate machine vocabulary for the owner; keep it compressed and precise between agents.

fields.title: Render and witness a flag-guarded surface
fields.problem: Two failure modes. (1) Reaching for a screenshot where an assertion would do — 'the path starts at the dock and never self-intersects' is a geometry assertion; 'the panel shows X given these props' is a component test. (2) For the part that needs an eye, hand-writing a throwaway capture script each run, re-hitting the same traps (a hidden browser tab suspends rendering and hangs the screenshot) and producing evidence no two runs agree on.
fields.approach: 1. Push machine facts down: geometry invariants and render/behaviour facts become tests; use DOM/computed-style inspection to turn an eyeballed fact into an assertion. What remains is the look. 2. Witness with a committed capability: the repo's Playwright/e2e harness for the desktop app, with deterministic settling (wait for app-reported settled state, never sleep), a visible or headless page, and deterministic rendering so the witness is repeatable. If no harness covers the surface, build one once rather than a per-run script. 3. Keep it feedback: build the look behind a flag, capture it, stand the experience up for the owner, and stop. Only the owner's attestation moves the look to done; the builder never self-signs it.
fields.statement: A visual builder checks its work by witnessing a flag-guarded surface, but the witness is FEEDBACK, never the proof: first turn every machine-checkable visual fact into a test, then witness only the irreducible look with the repo's committed capture harness, and stop for the owner's look verdict.
fields.tradeoffs: A committed harness is less nimble than a bespoke one-off script, but pays for itself by the second use. The sharper risk is the inverse over-reach: treating a green self-captured screenshot as if it proved the look.
fields.description: A visual builder's own screenshots are feedback, never a verdict: push machine-checkable visual facts into tests, witness the rest with a committed harness, and hand the owner a working surface to attest.

fields.why: Story-author owns WHAT, so a structural fork already has an owner who is not the human. In 0.2 a package-layout fork was put to the owner, who corrected: 'the answer to these questions should belong to story writer not to me'; routed to story-author it was decided cleanly and landed green. Escalating it spends the owner's scarcest channel on a question the corpus already routes elsewhere and stalls the work.
fields.title: Route structural forks to story-author, not the owner
fields.statement: A fork whose subject is the WORK HIERARCHY — which package owns what, dependency edges, where a module lives, story/capability boundaries, whether a new story is needed — is decided by the story-author role, not escalated to the owner. Raise it to the owner only if the structural call is genuinely irreversible, outward-facing, or unsettleable from the decision log.
fields.howToApply: When a unit hinges on a structural, package, dependency or boundary call, spawn story-author to decide and author it (plan_story / plan_capability), then record the decision (accepted when the owner directed it in the conversation). The discriminator is the SUBJECT of the fork, not your confidence: 'I'm unsure which package owns this' is still story-author's call.
fields.description: Package layout, dependency edges and story boundaries are the story-author's call, not the owner's.

fields.steps:
1. Ask what MAIN's code infers, not what your branch needs: find every query on main that names or infers the thing you would drop (an ON CONFLICT target errors the moment its index is gone).
2. Never swap in one edit: a drop+add in one landing has no safe moment - applied early it breaks every older writer, withheld it leaves your branch red.
3. EXPAND in its own PR: additive schema only, the old shape still standing, AND every writer moved to the new target.
4. MIGRATE in that same PR: backfill with values correct for existing rows; every statement a no-op on re-run, and the fresh-install path and the upgrade path must produce the identical shape.
5. CONTRACT in a later PR, once no running code still infers the old shape (installed apps included). When you cannot establish that, leave the overlap - a redundant index is cheap.
6. If no compatible overlap exists, name the break window (who breaks, for how long) and escalate; never take a silent one.
fields.title: Migrate a library schema: expand, migrate, contract
fields.trigger: You are about to change the project schema in a way that drops or narrows something: a primary key, a unique constraint or index an ON CONFLICT infers, a foreign-key target, a column, a NOT NULL. Purely additive changes (new table, new column with a default) do not arm it.
fields.surfaces: The library package's project schema and its apply-on-open; every writer whose SQL names a constraint; separate PRs through the merge ceremony.
fields.statement: The project schema is applied on every open of a project library, and more than one version of the code opens the same library: the app that follows merged main, your branch's tests and tools, a sibling session's branch, and a user's older installed app. So a change that drops or narrows something running code relies on lands in steps: EXPAND (add the new shape beside the old and move every writer onto it), MIGRATE (backfill, guarded, re-runnable), then CONTRACT (drop the old shape) in a later PR.
fields.description: A schema change that drops or narrows something lands as expand, then migrate, then contract, in separate PRs - never a one-shot swap.
fields.failureModes:
- A constraint swap treated as one atomic edit: in 0.2 a primary-key swap left the branch red against the shared store while applying it would have broken main's claim writes for every other session.
- Reading "idempotent" as "safe": a guarded, re-runnable swap is still incompatible with the code already running.
- Contracting in the same PR that expanded.
- Fresh-install and upgrade paths that diverge, so two openers disagree about what the table is.

fields.why: This is the problem storytree exists for. An operator running several agent sessions is flooded, not starved; the only options were 'read everything' (the operator is the bottleneck again) or 'trust it' (discovery deferred to runtime). A middle exists only if something takes a position on what deserves attention now. A position is a claim that can be examined and overruled, unlike a summary whose omissions look like absences. The owner's correction: storytree IS opinionated and MAY hide paths, but rarely — 99% of the time there is a visible way.
fields.title: Show what matters at the stage they are at
fields.statement: A surface shows the operator what matters AT THE STAGE THEY ARE ACTUALLY AT — the system holds an opinion about that and acts on it, including by hiding what this stage does not need — and because that opinion can be wrong, there is always one consistent way to overrule it.
fields.howToApply: Ask what stage the reader is at before asking what to show: at THIS stage, does this change what the operator does next? Rank before you hide; hiding is the expensive, declared exception with a stated reason. Never hide that you hid — the fact of an opinion stays visible, with an always-present escape hatch reachable from where the operator hit the wall, not buried in settings.
fields.description: A surface takes a position on what deserves the operator's attention now — and always leaves one way to overrule it.

fields.why: An agent works in a finite attention window. Every sentence that does not help it choose the next move competes with the sentences that do; low-signal guidance does not merely fail to help, it crowds out what would.
fields.title: Signal and noise
fields.statement: Judge any guidance an agent reads by its discriminatory power — signal lets the agent tell the correct action from the alternatives; noise consumes attention without adding that power — and author for high signal.
fields.howToApply: High signal is actionable, specific (concrete files, commands, decisions), verifiable, and grounded in the code as it is. Noise is meta-talk, stale context, generic philosophy and restatement. Per sentence ask: can I remove it without lowering the chance the task completes? Does it point to a specific action or criterion? Is it said elsewhere (link the one source)? Will it still be true later?
fields.description: Judge guidance by discriminatory power: keep what helps an agent choose the right move, cut the rest.

fields.why: The black-box complaint was never that tools show too little; it is that what they show is generated rather than measured — a narration by the same thing doing the work, structurally unable to contradict it, and most confident exactly where it is least informed. It is also what makes the surface's opinionatedness affordable: ranking measurements is triage; ranking guesses is a confident guess with fewer options.
fields.title: Signals must be real
fields.statement: Everything a surface shows is ANCHORED TO REAL CODE AND REAL TELEMETRY — a signal is a READING TAKEN FROM the system, never a DESCRIPTION OF the system produced alongside it.
fields.howToApply: For every element, name what it was read FROM — the file, the record, the event, the test run. If you cannot, it is decoration: remove it. Prefer an honest 'unknown' to a plausible placeholder. Beware a signal computed from its own subject: ask what state of the world would turn it red; if none, it measures nothing. Staleness is allowed; undisclosed staleness is not — a snapshot says when it was taken. Rollups of real readings are real; prose is fine unless it presents as a reading.
fields.description: Everything a surface shows is a reading taken from real code and telemetry, never a description generated alongside it.

fields.why: Source built ahead of a proving test is unproven surface: an interface with one implementation, a dependency no test demanded, a refactor smuggled into a fix all add behaviour no red test pinned, so the tests attest to less than what shipped.
fields.title: Slow growth: the minimum to green
fields.statement: Write the minimum source that turns the failing test (or the small cluster of tests you just wrote) green — no speculative abstraction, no speculative dependency, no wide refactor disguised as a fix.
fields.howToApply: Pick the red test(s); make the smallest change in the owning package that turns them green; iterate. Every test the source answers to exists before the source does. Smells: an interface with a single implementation, a package added without naming the test that demands it, a diff touching files no failing test reaches.
fields.description: Write the minimum source that turns the failing test green — no speculative abstraction, dependency or refactor.

fields.why: Premature splits fragment a journey and multiply seams; refusing to split leaves units whose outcome is a list and whose proof is two unrelated walkthroughs stapled together. Two falsifiable triggers make the call testable rather than aesthetic.
fields.title: The splitting rule
fields.statement: Split a story, capability or contract only when EITHER its outcome cannot be stated in one sentence without conjunctions, OR its proof does not share a common precondition and observable.
fields.howToApply: Tiebreakers — split if two or more hold: distinct REAL user populations (not role labels worn by the same person), two separate rebuild briefs, a spike mixed with delivery, an internal contradiction. Length is NEVER a splitting criterion. After deciding to split, re-check each side is still one coherent journey.
fields.description: Split a unit only when its outcome needs conjunctions or its proof shares no common precondition and observable; length never counts.

fields.steps:
1. Start it yourself from the right directory with the right runner (dev server, desktop app, built site). A bare shell line punted to the owner broke in his environment once (wrong cwd, a local dependency not on PATH) and he had to debug it before he could test; his direction was to have it up and running so he can simply test.
2. Probe, do not assume: an HTTP 2xx on the entry route, a rendered marker, or a screenshot of the actual surface. If it will not serve, that is yours to fix or escalate.
3. Hand over the confirmed link, the exact thing to open or try, and the specific question to rule on; the question itself goes on the arc as an open question.
4. Never record the owner's verdict yourself because you made it easy to give.
fields.title: Stage the owner's look
fields.trigger: A unit reaches a point only an owner look can settle (appearance, feel, a live check he must witness).
fields.surfaces: The session's own dev servers / app launch and the probe that confirms them; the handoff message; an open question on the arc.
fields.statement: When a unit needs the owner to look at, feel or try something running - a visual surface, an interaction, a desktop build - the session starts it, verifies it is genuinely serving, and hands the owner a confirmed-working URL or entry point plus a short "what to judge". A raw command is only a fallback. The owner still gives the verdict; you remove the friction, not the judgment.
fields.description: When the owner must see something running to judge it, start it yourself, prove it serves, and hand over a working link plus what to judge.
fields.failureModes:
- Handing over a command instead of a running experience.
- "I ran the start command so it is up" - the server never bound, the build 404s, or a hidden browser tab stalls.
- Signing the look-and-feel verdict yourself.
- Spinning up servers for every message: this is for the moment the owner must witness something.

fields.why: A stateful rule promoted to guidance misfires in every context lacking its hidden state, and guidance is read by every future session, so a wrong graduation spreads exactly as far as a right one. The asymmetry favours withholding: leaving a stateless item another round costs one round; graduating a stateful one costs every reader until someone notices.
fields.title: Stateless graduates, stateful stays
fields.statement: Only a STATELESS rule — one that applies the same way on every read, with no dependence on prior sessions, host paths or accumulated context — graduates into durable guidance; STATEFUL context stays where it is, and UNCERTAIN withholds.
fields.howToApply: When graduating memory into the library, classify each candidate: STATELESS → candidate; STATEFUL (a path, a date-bound state, a one-session recipe) → stays in memory; UNCERTAIN → withhold. State the classification in every proposal — it is the load-bearing logic, not a formality.
fields.description: Only stateless rules graduate from memory into library guidance; stateful context stays ephemeral, and uncertainty withholds.

fields.why: A test is only as good as the observable it pins. Checking that a file exists (not its contents), that a function was called (not what it produced), or that a flag is true (not the result it claims) gives a green with no proof behind it — and an agent rewarded for green will satisfy exactly that hollow signal. Fixtures fail the same way: a whole-module mock deletes the real library's runtime guards (0.2: 885/885 green while the real library threw), and hand-built small numbers cannot discriminate a rule that breaks at production scale.
fields.title: Test creation principles
fields.statement: A test must verify the actual outcome rather than a proxy for it — real content over existence, user-facing behaviour over implementation detail — and must genuinely fail if the behaviour it pins were removed.
fields.howToApply: The deletion check first: if the feature were removed, would this test fail? If not, it pins nothing. Assert produced content and behaviour, including the unhappy path; avoid permissive assertions (length > 0), success-flag-only checks, swallowed errors. Under minimal viable TDD a test earns its place by protecting a product behaviour — no tests of decision records, prose, retirements or repo structure. Prefer real collaborators (0.3's tests get a throwaway local Postgres); when you must mock, pin the options the real dependency requires and make fixture values span production magnitudes. Never assert a wall-clock duration — on a shared box it measures CPU starvation; use an injected clock. Make an environment-bound test's skip visible (a skip option, not an `if` around the declaration), so a test that did not run is never counted as proof.
fields.description: A test verifies the real outcome, not a proxy, and must fail if the behaviour it pins were removed.

fields.why: Two jobs get confused. Deciding whether something needs you is triage and is the system's job — making the operator click through a hierarchy to find out is 'review everything' with nicer graphics. Deciding how far to go is investigation and is the operator's — depth is only a cost when it is compulsory. The owner's words: 'you choose which rabbit hole to jump into and how far to go down.' A drill-down gives depth without selection; a search box gives selection without depth; neither is the in-between.
fields.title: The reader chooses the thread and the depth
fields.statement: TRIAGE IS PUSHED AND INVESTIGATION IS PULLED — the system decides WHAT NEEDS the operator's attention, and the operator decides WHICH thread to follow and HOW FAR DOWN it to go.
fields.howToApply: Separate the two jobs before designing either: triage arrives unbidden, investigation never does. Count clicks to a decision (target zero), not clicks to the bottom. Every level must answer something on its own — a level that exists only to be passed through is a toll. Offer more than one way in. Treat stopping as success. A suggestion of where to look next is fine; 'show more' of the same level is not another level.
fields.description: Triage is pushed and investigation is pulled: the system says what needs attention; the operator chooses which thread and how deep.

fields.why: When the resting view is derived from bounds, padding and a projection, there is always a true sentence available — this is what the function returns — which answers a question nobody asked. In 0.2 a projection change left half the modules on old assumptions and the map silently opened ~28x smaller; every piece was defensible, the composition nobody owned was not, and there was no stated framing for the new one to contradict. An undesigned view cannot be regressed.
fields.title: The resting view is designed, not fitted
fields.statement: The RESTING COMPOSITION of a visual surface — the camera, zoom and framing a reader arrives at — is a DESIGNED state someone chose and can defend. A camera or fit function that merely contains the content has computed a view, not designed one, and 'the fit computes it' never answers whether the view is right.
fields.howToApply: Ask who decided the framing, against what intent (how much of the whole is visible, what dominates, what the margins are for). Treat any change that moves the resting composition — projection maths, bounds, padding, camera elevation, a sizing constant — as a change to the composition, and give it the owner's look. When a view is derived, pin what it must satisfy: a stated share of the frame, a minimum on-screen size for the primary object, or a reference capture. Views the reader navigated to themselves are theirs, not the surface's.
fields.description: The composition a reader arrives at is a decision someone made; 'the fit function computes it' is not evidence it is right.

fields.why: The trees look like one repository and behave like several, and tools report success either way. In 0.2 a session wrote a whole increment (nine files) into the primary checkout while working in a worktree; its own `git status` was clean, so its honesty check passed while the edits landed on a divergent baseline. The read half is quieter: a session read a schema through the primary checkout's path and got a version two decisions old. Absolute paths copied from briefs and memory never look environment-specific, and subagents inherit the slip with the path.
fields.title: The same file in another tree is a different file
fields.statement: A repository checked out more than once — the primary checkout plus every worktree, and in 0.3's training-wheels period two repositories side by side — has one path per tree and different bytes behind each. Resolve every path against THIS session's own root, and never read another tree's content, clean status or green test as evidence about your branch.
fields.howToApply: Establish the root once from the session: `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` in your own directory. Treat any path from a brief, memory file or earlier session as a recollection. Worktrees live under the primary root, so 'starts with the primary path' proves nothing — the longest matching root wins. After a write, a clean status in your tree is not confirmation; check where it landed. Give every subagent your absolute root explicitly and check both trees when it returns. Before a read becomes a premise, know which commit that tree is on.
fields.description: In a worktree session, resolve every path against your own tree's root; another checkout's bytes and status are not evidence about your branch.

fields.why: A tightened validator can break fixtures or data anywhere that leaned on the old looser behaviour, and that surfaces at runtime, not at typecheck — so the change compiles, the owning package is green, and the break lands elsewhere. In 0.3 tests run only what a change can reach, so this is the case where you must widen the run deliberately. The sweep half: in 0.2 a migration searched for the tag `witness: human`, reported 'none remain', and missed five untagged items the parser defaulted to exactly that value — the blind spot pointed straight at the units the sweep existed for.
fields.title: Tightening a shared contract needs a full sweep
fields.statement: When a change makes a shared parser, schema or validator reject inputs it used to accept, run the tests of EVERY package that consumes it before landing — not just the owner's. And whenever a sweep will claim completeness, derive its scope by enumerating every unit and resolving each one's value through the real parser, never by searching for the marker.
fields.howToApply: Tightening (reject more)? Run `pnpm test` across all consumers of the contract, or the full suite; a red sibling blocks the landing. Loosening cannot break an existing fixture, so it does not trigger. For a sweep: enumerate the universe, parse each unit with the production parser, bucket by resolved value, and check the buckets sum to the total. Ask what an ABSENT value defaults to — if it defaults to the value you are sweeping for, a marker search misses every one.
fields.description: When a shared validator starts rejecting what it accepted, test every consumer; scope any completeness-claiming sweep by enumerating units, never by grepping a marker.

fields.why: A unit extracted for a single consumer is indirection with no reuse payoff: it adds a hop for every reader, splits authority between the unit and its lone consumer, and bets context budget on a future that may never come.
fields.title: Two-consumer extraction
fields.statement: Extract shared content into its own unit only when two or more CURRENT consumers share it — one consumer plus a hoped-for second is speculation, not extraction.
fields.howToApply: Count actual consumers before extracting and name them in the new note. Below two, leave the content where it lives. This is the complement of reference-dont-restate: that rule says link, don't copy, once a note exists; this one says when a note should exist at all.
fields.description: Extract shared content into its own note only when two or more current consumers share it.

fields.why: Chasing surface coverage authors unproven breadth — tests no red ever demanded — whereas a defect-driven list keeps every case earned by a real failure. This is the story-level form of minimal viable TDD, carried from 0.2's UAT practice (a CLI proven by running a few core commands, a store by a successful data pull).
fields.title: A story's proof proves the goal, not the surface
fields.statement: A story's end-to-end proof shows its OUTCOME — it does not cover the surface. Author the minimal case that proves the goal against real collaborators; the list grows only when a real defect earns a permanent regression case.
fields.howToApply: Ship one test that proves the story's goal end to end with real collaborators. Add a case only when a real defect surfaces, and keep it permanently. If a surface genuinely cannot be settled by code or a driver (a taste judgement), say so explicitly rather than skipping it silently — but an un-harnessed surface is a build task, not a reason to skip.
fields.description: Prove the story's outcome with the minimal end-to-end case; grow the list one case per real defect.

fields.why: A negative verdict is only worth something if something was checked. In 0.2 a research run with 128 of 714 agents hitting session limits scored ~63 true claims as refuted; a self-written coverage probe whose regex was corrupted by a shell heredoc reported 28/28 uncovered and reached an accepted decision; a scripted find-and-replace printed 'ok' while missing three sites that surfaced as later failures; a title parser that could not read `'a' + 'b'` stamped six real tests 0/6 covered. Each time the checker's blindness was laundered into a fact about the code.
fields.title: A check that could not run is unverified, not refuted
fields.statement: Before you cite or dismiss a checker's output, establish that it actually ran and could see what it reports on. A crashed, rate-limited, hung or never-launched check is UNVERIFIED, not a negative result. The same holds for instruments you write yourself: a scan that could never match reads as 'nothing found', a batch edit that matched nothing prints success, and a reader that silently skips items it cannot parse reports them as absent.
fields.howToApply: Look for the tells a check did not run: errors, timeouts, empty reasons, every panel dead, one item both confirmed and refuted — route those to unknown and re-run. For your own scan, pair it with a POSITIVE CONTROL (a case that must come back the other way) and read the control first. For a batch edit, use a tool that refuses on a non-match, or assert the applied count equals the expected count. For a reader, return a count of what it could not read beside what it could. Report an unknown's size rather than shrinking it by widening a predicate. And the mirror: do not REFUSE on an unknown unless a wrong answer would actually be believed — disclose it instead.
fields.description: A verdict from a checker that did not run, could not match, or could not read an item is unknown — never a negative.

fields.why: Write tools can return success without the content landing (path normalisation, the wrong worktree, a sandbox quirk, a store write that hung or was overwritten by a sibling session). The reflex in 0.2 was to silently fall back to a shell heredoc, which hid the failure: nobody learned the tool misbehaved and the symptom recurred unnamed next session.
fields.title: Verify an edit persisted, or escalate
fields.statement: When your deliverable depends on a write having landed — a source file, a test, a library note edit, a decision — read it back and confirm the intended content is there before you report it. If it did not persist, report that explicitly before applying any fallback; a silent workaround that hides the failure is banned.
fields.howToApply: Discriminator: would my summary lie if this write were not there? Then read it back (the file from your own tree, or the note via `storytree library read`, or its `history`). On failure — unchanged, absent, truncated — state what you intended and what you observed, then recover. The thing to preserve is the visibility of the failure, not the success of the recovery. Scratch files are out of scope.
fields.description: Read back every write your report depends on; if it did not land, say so before any workaround.

fields.why: A gated judgment is worse than an ungated one: ungated, a skipped ceremony is visibly missing; gated, every session performs it at the cheapest shape that satisfies the predicate, and the green check becomes evidence it was done. In 0.2 a check that an amended decision mentioned its amender's number was built and then deleted, because pasting the number satisfied it while the real obligation — an editorial note on what moved — went undone. A ceremony that must produce something will produce something, so the honest 'nothing to report' has to stay free.
fields.title: A compliance gate turns a judgment ceremony into theatre
fields.statement: Do not enforce a judgment ceremony (a retro, a curation pass, an escalation, an annotation that says which clause moved) with a CI check, test, marker or counter. A check can only read a proxy for having done it — a file exists, a field is non-empty, an item was filed — and every such proxy is producible without the judgment. The check then teaches authors that producing the proxy discharges the obligation, and reports green over the theatre it created.
fields.howToApply: Before proposing a check for a ceremony, ask in order: (1) What would it actually read? If that is a mechanical fact (does it parse, does the id exist, does the generated file match the library), a check is right and this rule does not apply. (2) Can the proxy be produced without the judgment? Write the cheapest compliance you can; that is what the check will teach. (3) Can the honest null ('nothing here') be scored for free? If not, the check manufactures findings. Then name what does hold the ceremony — a reviewed PR, a librarian round, a later session — or say plainly that nothing does. This never licenses skipping a check that exists, and argues against no mechanical-fact check.
fields.description: A ceremony whose value is a judgment cannot be enforced by a check — a check reads only a proxy, and every proxy can be produced without the judgment.

fields.why: Such a change is cheap to undo, but it deletes the evidence that would later say 'undo it', and it improves exactly the numbers a retro reads — fewer checks, less wall clock, fewer escalations — so it registers as a win. There is no run in which an instrument reports that it was the thing that changed. 0.2 retired sixteen gate checks and narrowed several triggers this way; each was defensible, and all were the one move whose error the system cannot observe about itself.
fields.title: A decision that blinds an instrument escalates inline
fields.statement: A change that REMOVES, NARROWS or WEAKENS a signal the owner relies on — deleting a CI check, narrowing what a test or check covers, raising an escalation bar, turning a blocking check advisory, dropping a reviewing seat's model tier, hiding something from a board — is decided WITH the owner before it lands, not reported afterwards. Reversibility is not the test for this class.
fields.howToApply: Ask of your own change before landing: after this, is there anything the owner could previously have learned that they now cannot? If yes or unsure, escalate inline — usually one paragraph naming what stops being visible and what you propose to watch instead. A signal is anything the owner reads to learn something is wrong: a check, its trigger or scope, a threshold, who reviews, what a board surfaces. Weakening counts, not only removal. Whether the signal deserves to exist is a legitimate question; this rule only says the answer is the owner's, taken before it goes dark.
fields.description: A decision that removes, narrows or weakens a signal the owner relies on goes to the owner before it lands, however reversible it looks.

fields.why: In 0.2 a 'NOT built' note sat byte-identical in a source header across four landing PRs; four sessions read it and carried it forward. Promoted into a decision record it turned out to be 'decided against', not 'not yet done'. Separately, a forward-looking sentence in an arc's landing log went false, the next session read it as settled state, and nearly authored a duplicate. Nothing degrades while such a note sits there, so no surface ever shows that a decision is waiting.
fields.title: A deferral recorded without a status reads as pending work
fields.statement: A deferral — a decision NOT to build, or a fork left open — is settled only when it lives in a record that carries a STATUS and an OWNER. Written as prose into a source comment, a PR description or an append-only landing note, it cannot be told apart from unfinished work, so every later reader re-inherits it instead of settling it.
fields.howToApply: When you are about to write, or you read, 'not built', 'deferred', 'left for later' or 'pending X', ask what the container can record: could a reader months out tell wanted-but-unbuilt from decided-against, and whose name is on the answer? A comment or a landing note cannot. In an append-only record also ask: when this sentence stops being true, what changes it? If nothing, it does not belong there. The remedy is promotion, not verification: a decision that will outlive the unit becomes a decision note; an owner's call becomes an open question on the arc; decided-but-unbuilt work becomes an increment on its arc. Leave a pointer where the prose was, not a copy.
fields.description: A decision not to build, written into a medium with no status and no owner, cannot be told apart from unfinished work — promote it into a status-bearing record.

fields.why: In 0.2 a 'NOT built' note sat byte-identical in a source header across four landing PRs; four sessions read it and carried it forward. Promoted into a decision record it turned out to be 'decided against', not 'not yet done'. Separately, a forward-looking sentence in an arc's landing log went false, the next session read it as settled state, and nearly authored a duplicate. Nothing degrades while such a note sits there, so no surface ever shows that a decision is waiting.
fields.title: A deferral recorded without a status reads as pending work
fields.statement: A deferral — a decision NOT to build, or a fork left open — is settled only when it lives in a record that carries a STATUS and an OWNER. Written as prose into a source comment, a PR description or an append-only landing note, it cannot be told apart from unfinished work, so every later reader re-inherits it instead of settling it.

A comment or a landing note cannot. In an append-only record also ask: when this sentence stops being true, what changes it? If nothing, it does not belong there. The remedy is promotion, not verification: a decision that will outlive the unit becomes a decision note; an owner's call becomes an open question on the arc; decided-but-unbuilt work becomes an increment on its arc. Leave a pointer where the prose was, not a copy.
fields.description: A decision not to build, written into a medium with no status and no owner, cannot be told apart from unfinished work — promote it into a status-bearing record.

fields.title: A measured claim carries the method that produced it
fields.problem: Numbers on a moving surface are supposed to change; the defect is that a later reader cannot tell from the note whether a figure was a reproducible measurement or a one-off snapshot, so before checking it they must reconstruct the measurement by guessing what was counted. In 0.2 an audit found 2 of 4 open questions drifted, one moving from 'n=1, self-measured' to 'n=43 sessions, 1 independent hit' within three days, unnoticed until someone went looking. The author is the only party who holds the method for free.
fields.approach: Beside each live figure, in the same field (not a footnote — a method kept elsewhere drifts from the number it describes), name: (1) the instrument, runnable verbatim — e.g. `storytree library list question`; (2) the sample and what it counts; (3) the moment, when the surface moves independently of any diff. At re-verification, the annotation is the instruction: re-run what it names; if it names no instrument, re-measure rather than re-read. When the figure moved, correct it in place AND re-stamp the method. Do NOT annotate figures that are not readings of a moving surface — a count fixed by a decision, a quoted constant — that is noise that trains readers to skip the annotation.
fields.statement: Any live, measured figure written into a durable note — an open question's stakes, an arc's intent or end state, a re-verification — is written together with its METHOD: the command or query that produced it, the sample (n, and n of WHAT), and when it was taken. If there was no instrument, say so: 'self-measured', 'eyeballed', 'filer's self-report'.
fields.tradeoffs: A parenthetical per figure, written while the author holds the method for free, against a reconstruction every later reader pays. It detects nothing and makes no claim true — it only makes every drift check cheaper. Nothing enforces it; a check keyed on backticks or 'n=' would be trivially satisfiable.
fields.description: A live number written into a durable note travels with how it was measured, so the next reader can re-run it instead of reconstructing it.

fields.why: In 0.2 an implementing agent built a described-but-uncontracted slice three times on one capability, even though the passage carried a plain not-yet-contracted label; each run passed honestly on the test it wrote, and the briefed contract showed up merely as uncovered. Deleting the future-slice prose and re-running built the briefed contract first time.
fields.title: A spec body describes only what it contracts
fields.statement: A capability's body carries only behaviour that is under contract. Anything described concretely enough to implement will be read by the implementing agent as something to build, and it outweighs the brief because it is the more specific thing in context. Labelling a passage 'later' or 'not yet contracted' does not defuse it; the only reliable fence is its absence. Direction and future slices belong on the story or on an arc's increments.
fields.howToApply: Before handing a capability to an agent (or yourself) to implement, read its body as a to-do list and strike anything implementable that is not a contract. Move durable intent to the story and sequencing to an arc increment. If an uncontracted slice has already been built, adopt it as a real contract so the work is kept, and remove every remaining mention of it from the body so the next run is not re-baited.
fields.description: An implementing agent reads a capability's body as instruction: a concretely described but uncontracted behaviour gets built instead of the contract it was asked for.

fields.why: Accepted decisions are what a new session calibrates to, so stale-but-accepted prose is read as live guidance — even an answer found in a decision may be dead. A correction left undone misleads every future reader, while removing overtaken prose costs nothing the history does not already hold. In 0.2 hundreds of amended decisions carried no note in their own body, and well-annotated ones still opened with the false sentence, so readers stopped at it. Escalating instead of correcting is free for the session and costly for the owner.
fields.title: Accepted decisions carry no stale prose
fields.statement: Every accepted decision in the current set is true in full. The moment a claim in one is overtaken, make it true again, choosing the operation by intent: if the DECISION did not change, CORRECT the body in place (the library's history keeps the prior text); if it did, write a NEW decision that supersedes the old, which then reads as superseded and stays as a browsable record. A decision that narrows or retires a clause of a standing one annotates that clause in the target, in the same landing. Durable cross-cutting guidance found in a decision body is rehomed into the principle, definition or pattern that owns it.
fields.howToApply: Ask whether the reasoning a clause rests on still holds; 'accepted' only proves nobody has checked. Then ask: did the decision change? No → edit in place. Yes → new decision with a supersedes edge. For a narrowed clause, put the note where the clause OPENS (who amended, when, what is dead, what replaced it) — a false opening sentence with its correction six lines below still misleads. A plain 'this rests on that' link obliges no annotation and never makes its target load-bearing. Status flips, edge fixes and typos are in-place too. When in doubt, treat it as a re-decision or ask; never silently rewrite what was decided.
fields.description: An accepted decision is true in full: overtaken content is corrected in place, a genuine re-decision supersedes, and a narrowed clause is annotated where it sits.

fields.steps:
1. Ask, do not infer: the first line of `pnpm test` is the `scope:` decision; `pnpm test -- --scope` prints it and runs nothing. `--full` forces everything; `--only=<pkg>` and `--rerun-failed` re-run just part.
2. The change set is merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) against the working tree, untracked files included; each file maps to its package, then dependents are added by declared dependency OR by a relative path in code that reaches another package.
3. It fails wide: a root file, any package.json, the lockfile, scripts/**, a file in no package, a missing origin/main, or no change at all runs everything. A root path is narrowed only once its test-time readers were measured, never by guess.
4. There is ONE decider (scripts/test-scope.mjs). Never write a second classifier for CI or a tool - two that agree today drift tomorrow, and a local pass stops predicting a CI pass.
5. If your change makes a package read another package's files with no dependency or relative-path edge the scope can see, declare the edge - otherwise a change there skips your tests and main goes red later.
6. Pushes to main run full (merge-base is HEAD itself); an automerge makes no push run, so a narrow PR's full proof comes from the next push to main.
fields.title: Affected-only test scope
fields.trigger: Every `pnpm test` run, locally and in CI. Read this when asking why a run tested only some packages, when adding code that reads a file in another package, or when main goes red soon after a narrow merge.
fields.surfaces: `pnpm test` (scripts/test.mjs, scripts/test-scope.mjs), CI's `pnpm test` step on three OSes, `.pgtest/last-run.json` for re-runs.
fields.statement: `pnpm test` runs only the workspace packages holding a changed file plus every package that depends on them, and CI runs the very same command, so a local run and CI decide identically. Anything the workspace graph cannot account for runs everything. A narrow green proves the reached packages, not the workspace.
fields.description: How `pnpm test` narrows to the packages a change can reach, what forces the full run, and how to read a narrow green.
fields.failureModes:
- Reading a narrow green as a full-workspace proof.
- A cross-package file read with no edge: the one shape that lets an untested change merge.
- Quietly loosening a fail-wide rule to save minutes.
- Moving code into its own package to shrink a run: dependents still run it; packaging buys a boundary, not a smaller suite.

fields.rule: Some verdicts are the owner's by nature: "it looks right", "it works live", "this spend is fine". An agent may prepare them — stand the experience up, verify it serves, hand over a working link and what to look at — but it never records the verdict itself, never marks work healthy on its own say-so, and never reports "attested" for something only it has seen. Where a test can prove the behaviour, prove it that way instead; where none can, the gap is the owner's to close.
fields.title: An agent never self-attests
fields.statement: An agent never grants itself an owner-only attestation; it stages the experience and the owner signs.
fields.enforcedBy: Discipline. 0.3 has no signed-verdict spine; the owner's sign-off is given in person or as the answer to an open question, and nothing mechanical detects a self-granted one.
fields.description: A verdict only the owner can give — a look, a feel, a live check, a spend — is never granted by the agent that did the work.
fields.failureMode: An agent vouches for its own unproven work, so a surface with no honest test reads as healthy and the proof means nothing — the reason 0.2 kept attestations in a log that could never reach healthy.
